## V-46: the two floors differ because I changed the estimator. The manuscript's .771 is not wrong; my code was.

**Numbers.** All-length bAbI task-1 floor under my code path: .316/.328/.348 = .3307, against the manuscript's
.7713 -- deltas -.455/-.443/-.423, so DOES NOT REPRODUCE by the registered bar. Short-only .3622, long-only
.1983, all-length at the larger draw .3310. Majority-class rates .188/.202/.235/.187, so the short and all-length
probes learn something beyond the prior (+.14 to +.16) and the LONG-only probe learns NOTHING beyond it (-.037).

**Cause, found by diffing the two implementations rather than by guessing.**
  v30.py and v13.Floor:  idx = am.sum(-1) - 1 ; H[arange, idx]      -- the LAST non-pad token's state
  v43.py / v45.py / v46.py (mine):  masked MEAN over all tokens
Both are legitimate probes and they measure different things. On bAbI the last token sits immediately after
"Where is Mary?", so in a causal model its state is the one used to generate the answer; a mean over the whole
story is far weaker. That is the whole .44. On arena C the two happen to land close (mean-pool .4940 at depth two
against v13's .5153), because a single token cannot carry that binary task either way.

**So the verdict stands as printed and its cause is the opposite of what the entry was written to test.** I
registered V-46 to find out whether the manuscript's .771 was wrong. It is not. What is wrong is that V-43, V-45
and V-46 all used a floor the paper does not use, and I did not notice while writing three preregs that leaned on
comparability with the paper's numbers. The manuscript needs no change on account of .771.

**What this does to the runs that used the wrong floor.**
  V-43's depth-3 result is UNAFFECTED in its core claim: probe_argmax equalling parser to four decimals is an
    arm-versus-arm equality and no floor enters it. Its headroom BAR did use the mean-pool floor, and the bar
    outcome is robust to the swap at depth two (hi = .8977 mean-pool versus .8921 last-token), but depth three
    has not been checked with the paper's estimator and will be.
  V-45's bar (a) -- "the baseline has purchase" -- FAILED for a reason I manufactured. The paper's estimator has
    .771 of purchase on bAbI; mine had .36. So V-45's "NO USABLE BASELINE" verdict is correct about what it
    measured and uninformative about the question it was asked. It gets rerun, not relabelled.
  V-45's POSITIVE half is untouched and does not depend on any floor: with the identity head trained only on
    stories of at most six statements, the chain reaches 1.0000 on held-out ten-statement stories with 5.33
    distinct locations, span identity 1.0000, three of three seeds.

**One thing V-46 found that is worth keeping regardless.** The long-only probe is BELOW its own majority-class
rate. Whatever the estimator, a pooled-state readout has nothing on ten-statement stories. If the last-token
probe behaves the same way, the contrast V-44 said arena C could not supply is available on bAbI after all --
which is exactly what the rerun tests.

**Tally.** Twenty-four predictions tested today, twenty failed -- I predicted V-46 would reproduce. Eight
apparatus or specification faults disclosed, this being the eighth and the third in which a bar of mine could not
answer the question it was written for.

## V-47 prereg: V-45 rerun with the paper's own floor estimator, plus V-43's bar rechecked. Before any code.

**Why.** V-46 established that my mean-pool floor is not the paper's floor: v13.Floor and v30.py read the LAST
non-pad token, which on bAbI is the state immediately after "Where is Mary?" and therefore the one a causal model
uses to answer. V-45's bar (a) -- "the baseline has purchase" -- was tested against my weaker estimator and
failed for that reason. This rerun uses the paper's estimator throughout, so the bars mean what they were written
to mean.

**Two halves, one script, both floors computed the paper's way (last non-pad token).**
  (A) bAbI task 1, story-length extrapolation, exactly V-45's design: identity head and probe trained on stories
      of at most six statements, evaluated on those and on held-out stories of at least ten. Arms floor, parser,
      probe_argmax. Bars (a), (b), (c) verbatim from V-45's prereg at 094cc5d, unchanged.
  (B) Arena C, the floor at depths two, three and four computed with v13.Floor's estimator, so V-43's headroom
      bar can be rechecked against the number the paper actually uses. probe_argmax and parser are read back as
      BANKED from v43_logs/v43_BANKED.json and not recomputed.

**Bars for (A), restated verbatim so there is no drift.** Per bucket H = parser - floor, admission H >= 0.20.
(a) THE BASELINE HAS PURCHASE iff the SHORT-bucket floor is >= 0.70 in 3/3.
(b) EXTRAPOLATES iff probe_argmax on LONG >= floor_long + 0.90 H_long in 3/3 AND >= 0.90 x its own SHORT accuracy
    in 3/3.
(c) THE CONTRAST HOLDS iff the probe's LONG accuracy is at least 0.10 below its SHORT accuracy in 3/3.
A positive result requires (a) AND (b) AND (c). (b) without (c) is "extrapolates, no contrast".

**Bar for (B).** V-43's depth-3 claim SURVIVES THE ESTIMATOR SWAP iff probe_argmax at depth three, banked, is
still >= floor_3 + 0.90 (parser_3 - floor_3) in 3/3 with the last-token floor. If it does not survive, the
manuscript paragraph written from V-43 must be corrected, and I will say that the claim was scaled against a
floor the paper does not use.

**Also reported, no bar.** Majority-class rate per bucket, and the probe's training accuracy, since V-46 showed
the long-bucket mean-pool probe fell BELOW its own prior and I want that visible for the last-token probe too.

**Predictions on the record.** (a) holds, around .77 as in V-30. (c) holds: V-46 found a pooled readout has
nothing on ten-statement stories, below its own prior, and I expect the last-token probe to degrade with length
as well, though less severely. (b) holds, since V-45 already measured 1.0000 on long stories and no floor enters
that number. (B) survives. Twenty-four predictions tested today and twenty failed; three of the four that held
were ones where the mechanism was nameable in advance, as (b) and (B) are here. (a) and (c) are the ones I could
be wrong about, and (c) is the whole point -- it is the contrast V-44 said arena C could not supply.

**What a negative on (c) means.** If the last-token probe holds its accuracy on long stories, then pooled-state
readouts handle bAbI length robustly, there is no compositional contrast on this substrate either, and the
paper's "why prefer a symbolic route" section stays as weak as it currently is. I would report that and stop
looking for the contrast on bAbI.

## V-47 EXTRAPOLATES + CONTRAST HOLDS -- the compositional contrast, on a baseline that demonstrably works

**Half (A): bAbI task 1, story length, the paper's floor estimator (last non-pad token).**
  bucket   probe_argmax          parser                floor (paper's estimator)   span identity
  short    1.000 1.000 1.000     1.000 1.000 1.000     .820 .8283 .8083  = .8189   1.0000
  long     1.000 1.000 1.000     1.000 1.000 1.000     .625 .640  .625   = .6300   1.0000
Short = at most six statements, the training distribution. Long = at least ten, held out, mean 5.33 distinct
locations against 3.12 in short. 540 train / 600 short eval / 200 long eval.

**All three registered bars hold, in three of three seeds.**
(a) BASELINE HAS PURCHASE: short floor .820/.8283/.8083, all >= .70. The probe genuinely does this task at the
    training length -- which is what V-44 found arena C could not give at any training depth.
(b) EXTRAPOLATES: probe_argmax on long = 1.0000, above floor_long + 0.90 H_long, and equal to its own short
    accuracy. The identity head never saw a story longer than six statements. Span identity stays 1.0000, so the
    head is recognising symbols in contexts nearly twice as long as any it trained on.
(c) CONTRAST HOLDS: the same probe loses .195/.1883/.1833 from short to long, every seed past the .10 bar.
So: a baseline that works at training length loses nineteen points when the stories get longer, and the discrete
handover does not move. This is the compositional evidence the paper has been missing, and it is on natural text.

**Half (B): V-43's depth-3 claim SURVIVES THE ESTIMATOR SWAP.** Recomputing the arena-C floor the paper's way at
depths two, three and four leaves probe_argmax clearing the .90-headroom bar at depth three in three of three.
So the V-43 paragraph already in the manuscript does not need correcting for the floor I got wrong.

**A prereg/scorer mismatch, disclosed.** The prereg says the .20 admission gate applies "per bucket"; the scorer
applied it to the LONG bucket only. The short bucket's headroom is .1811, under the gate. It changes nothing
here and I am not treating it as a rescue: (a) is a threshold on the probe itself, and (c) compares the SAME arm
across two buckets. Neither uses the short bucket's headroom, and no arm-versus-arm comparison is made there.
But the registered text and the code disagreed and the disagreement is mine.

**Also standing from V-46, and it now reads differently.** The mean-pool probe fell BELOW its own majority-class
rate on long stories (-.037). The last-token probe does not collapse that far -- .63 against a .235 prior -- so
the length effect is a real degradation of a working readout rather than a floor artifact. That distinction is
what makes (c) worth stating.

**Prediction outcome.** I predicted (a), (b), (c) and (B) all hold, and all four did. Twenty-eight predictions
tested today, twenty failed. The four that held in a row here were the ones where the mechanism was nameable in
advance: a per-span head cannot see story length, a per-hop algebra decays only with binding count, and a single
token summarising a longer story must lose information.

## V-48 prereg: the last natural-text floor I computed with the wrong estimator. Before any code.

**Why this before any new experiment.** V-46 established the paper's floor convention: the last non-pad token, as
v13.Floor and v30.py compute it. V-47 half (B) rechecked the arena-C depth floors under that convention and the
V-43 verdict survived. Auditing which manuscript floors came from my mean-pool code leaves exactly one
outstanding: v37.py, the bAbI task-2 two-hop run, whose floor is quoted in the manuscript as "$0.203$ for a
six-way linear probe on the pooled state". On bAbI the two estimators differ by forty points (V-46: .331 against
.771), so .203 is very likely not the number the paper's own convention would give, and it sets the admission gate
for a result already written into Results and cited in the Discussion.

**Not in question.** V-37b's probe_argmax and parser are arm-versus-arm at 1.000 and no floor enters them; the
94.6% expressiveness ceiling is a property of the oracle bundle, not of any probe. Only the floor, the headroom,
and the sentence quoting .203 are at issue.

**Setup.** Rerun v37b's floor arm ONLY, with the estimator swapped to the last non-pad token and nothing else
changed: same task, same build(), same expressible-subset filter, same seeds 42/123/456, same probe epochs.
probe_argmax, parser, the subset sizes and the ceiling are read back as BANKED from v37_logs/v37b.json and never
recomputed. Also reported: the majority-class rate on the expressible evaluation subset, which V-37b never
measured, so a high floor can be told apart from a skewed label prior.

**Bars.**
(a) THE QUOTED NUMBER STANDS iff the last-token floor is within 0.05 of .2032 in 3/3. Then .203 was right by
    accident of convention-agreement and the manuscript needs no change.
(b) THE QUOTED NUMBER IS WRONG iff the last-token floor is more than 0.10 above .2032 in 3/3. The manuscript
    sentence gets corrected to the paper's own convention, the headroom is restated, and I say plainly that the
    number came from an estimator the paper does not use.
(c) ADMISSION SURVIVES iff, under the corrected floor, parser - floor >= 0.20 in 3/3. If it does not, the
    depth-two natural-text comparison is VOID by the paper's own gate and the paragraph must say so -- which
    would remove a result the manuscript currently presents as a headline.
(d) GRADED in between on (a)/(b): report both and reconcile before editing.

**Prediction on the record.** (b) and (c): the last-token floor lands well above .203 -- I would guess .55 to .75,
since the final position sits right after "Where is the football?" -- and the admission still survives because
parser is at 1.000, so any floor below .80 leaves headroom over .20. Twenty-eight predictions tested today and
twenty failed; this one I would rather have measured than guessed, which is why it is registered rather than
assumed.

**What makes this worth doing rather than adding a new result.** A wrong floor in a headline sentence is the exact
defect class this paper's audit half documents, and I introduced it. Finding it myself, before submission, is
worth more than another positive.

## V-48 THE QUOTED NUMBER STANDS -- and the estimator audit is now complete

**Numbers.** bAbI task 2, expressible subset 775 train / 420 eval (identical to the banked V-37b subsets).
Last-non-pad-token floor .2524/.2357/.2476 = .2452, against the .2032 quoted in the manuscript: within .05 in
three of three seeds, so bar (a) holds and no manuscript change is needed. Majority-class rate on the same
subset .2048. Banked parser 1.0000, so headroom .7548 and the admission gate survives with room to spare.

**My prediction was wrong, and the reason is worth keeping.** I predicted .55 to .75, reasoning from task 1 where
the last-token floor is .771. It is .245, four points above its own label prior. The final-position shortcut
works exactly when the task is ONE hop: task 1 asks "Where is Mary?" and the state right after the question
already carries the answer, while task 2 asks "Where is the football?" and needs object to holder to location, so
the final position cannot bridge it. That connects the two tasks rather than just correcting a guess, and it is
the mechanism behind the forty-point gap V-46 found between the estimators on task 1 and the four-point gap here.

**Which makes the task-2 result stronger than it was.** Its floor is near chance under BOTH pooling operators, so
the 1.000-against-.203 comparison is not an artifact of having picked a weak baseline. That is worth one sentence
in the manuscript, and it forecloses the obvious referee question about floors computed with different poolings.

**The estimator audit is complete.** Every floor the manuscript quotes is now either computed with the paper's
own convention or verified equivalent under it: arena-C depths (V-47 half B, rechecked, verdict unchanged), bAbI
task 1 (v30, last-token by construction), the task-1 length buckets (V-47, last-token), task 2 (this entry,
verified equivalent), V-35 and V-36 (banked .7713 from v30), V-41 and V-42 (v13.Floor). The audit opened because
V-45 failed a bar for a reason I created; it closes with one number corrected in the ledger, none in the
manuscript, and one result strengthened.

**Tally.** Twenty-nine predictions tested today, twenty-one failed.

## V-49 prereg: the baseline we never ran -- just ask the model. Before any code.

**Why this is the most important remaining experiment, and why it should have been first.** Every comparison in
this paper is against a linear probe on frozen states. Not one is against the obvious thing a practitioner would
do: prompt the frozen model and read its answer. On bAbI task 1 that may already be near ceiling, in which case
"supervised handover reaches 1.000" is not evidence that the algebra buys anything, and the paper's practical
claim collapses to nothing. A referee will ask for this. I am asking for it first.

**Setup.** Phi-2, the same instances the mechanism arms were scored on, no fine-tuning and no probe.
  zeroshot     the story, the question, and "Answer:" -- next-token distribution restricted to the six location
               words, arg-max taken. Restricting to the legal answer set is generous to the baseline and is the
               fair comparison, since our arms also choose among six locations.
  fewshot      the same with four worked examples prepended, drawn from the TRAINING split only.
  Both on bAbI task 1 (all lengths, and the short/long buckets from V-47) and on task 2's expressible subset.
Reported: accuracy per cell, and for task 1 the short/long split so the length contrast has the same baseline.

**Bars.**
(a) THE ALGEBRA ADDS NOTHING iff the better prompting arm is >= 0.95 on task 1 all-lengths in 3/3 draws. Then
    the handover's 1.000 is a rounding difference over free inference, the paper may NOT claim a practical gain
    anywhere on task 1, and I write that into the Discussion as the headline limitation.
(b) THE ALGEBRA ADDS SOMETHING MEASURABLE iff the better prompting arm is <= 0.80 on task 1 all-lengths in 3/3.
    Then a supervised handover at 1.000 is a real gap over prompting and the paper may say so, scoped to this
    task.
(c) GRADED in between: report the number and claim nothing either way.
(d) SEPARATELY, on length: if prompting degrades from short to long by less than the 0.183-0.195 the frozen-state
    probe lost, then the length contrast in the paper is a statement about PROBES and not about language models,
    and the manuscript must say that the contrast does not extend to the model's own inference.
(e) SEPARATELY, on task 2: report prompting accuracy against the handover's 1.000 and the .245 floor, no bar.

**Prediction on the record.** (b) fails and (a) is close: I expect few-shot prompting on bAbI task 1 to land
between .85 and .97, because task 1 is a single-hop lookup in a short story and this is exactly what a 2.7B model
does well. Which would mean the honest answer to "does the algebra make the model better" is no on task 1, and
the paper's value is the audit and the mechanism rather than any capability gain. I would rather register that
expectation and be shown wrong than let a referee discover it.

**What I will not do with the result.** If (a) comes out I will not retreat to "but our arms use fewer
parameters" or "but the algebra is interpretable" without measuring those too. The claim under test is capability,
and if the answer is no, the paper says no.

## V-49: the baseline we never ran. One claim strengthened, one narrowed, and the verdict is fragile.

**Numbers (Phi-2, next-token restricted to the six single-token location words -- all six were usable, so no
instance was dropped; three prompt draws).**
  cell                     zeroshot                 fewshot (4)                banked handover / floor
  task1 all                .792 .792 .792  .7920    .8127 .758 .718  .7627     1.0000 / .7713
  task1 short              .850 .850 .850  .8500    .8467 .7667 .7033 .7722    1.0000 / .8189
  task1 long               .700 .700 .700  .7000    .770 .720 .780  .7567      1.0000 / .6300
  task2 (expressible)      .386 .386 .386  .3860    .364 .404 .492  .4200      1.0000 / .2452
Zero-shot is deterministic, hence identical across draws; few-shot varies with the exemplars and, on task 1,
HURTS on average.

**Verdict by the registered bars: ADDS SOMETHING MEASURABLE on task 1 -- and it holds by eight thousandths.**
The bar is "better prompting arm <= 0.80 in 3/3" and the better arm is zero-shot at .792. Few-shot's best single
draw is .8127, above the bar. Had I defined "better arm" as the best single draw rather than the better mean, this
would have come out GRADED. I am reporting the verdict as the prereg defines it AND reporting that it is fragile,
because a reader who recomputes it the other way gets a different answer.

**The solid result is task 2, and V-48 explains why.** Prompting reaches .386 zero-shot and .420 few-shot against
the handover's 1.000 -- a gap of about fifty-eight points, on the expressible subset where the algebra is being
asked only what it can express. V-48 showed the final-position state carries the answer when the question is ONE
hop and not when it is two; prompting is exactly that state being read by the model itself, so a two-hop question
is where the model's own shortcut runs out and where structure has something to add. That is the strongest
capability evidence in this paper and it is a two-hop-specific claim.

**And one claim is NARROWED by this run, against my own abstract.** On length, zero-shot degrades .15 from short
to long while the frozen-state probe lost .183 to .195. The model's own inference is MORE length-robust than the
probe. By the registered reading (d), the length contrast is therefore a statement about PROBES and not about
language models, and the manuscript must say so. I put that contrast into the abstract one iteration ago; the
abstract sentence is literally true as written (it names the probe) but a reader will generalise it, so it needs
the qualifier or it needs to go.

**An unexpected unification worth keeping.** Zero-shot task 1 is .792 and the last-token probe floor is .771 --
within two points. The probe reads the same state the model generates from, so this paper's "floor" has been,
all along, a proxy for what the model does unaided. That makes every floor comparison in the paper fairer than I
knew, and it should be said explicitly rather than left as a coincidence.

**The comparison still missing, and it is the one a referee will ask for.** Prompting is unsupervised; the
handover is supervised. The fair opponent for a supervised method is a supervised baseline, and on bAbI we have
only the linear probe. LoRA is measured on the synthetic arenas (where it beats the module) and never on bAbI.
Registered next as V-50.

**Tally.** Thirty predictions tested today, twenty-one failed. I predicted prompting would land .85-.97 and it
landed .792 on task 1 and .386 on task 2, so I was wrong in the direction that favours the paper -- which is the
direction I trust least and checked hardest.

## V-50 prereg: train the language model ITSELF through the VSA. Before any code.

**The objection this answers, and the half of it that is right.** The standing objection is that no improvement was
seen because the VSA was not in the training loop. Half of that is already tested and is the paper's central
negative: the `spans` and `frozen_cont` arms train a projection WITH gradients flowing through bundling,
unbinding and cleanup, and they reach chance in every synthetic arena and 37.6% of headroom at depth two on bAbI.
The other half is untested and the objection is correct about it: in every run in this paper the LANGUAGE MODEL IS
FROZEN. We have never backpropagated the binding objective into the model. So "the model learns to place symbols
where they bind well" has never been given a chance, and that is the strongest form of the hypothesis.

**Arms, on bAbI task 1 (all lengths) and task 2 (expressible subset), Phi-2, LoRA r=8 on the attention
projections, seeds 42/123/456, the same training instances every other arm used.**
  lora_direct        LoRA fine-tuned with cross-entropy on the answer location token. No VSA anywhere. This is
                     the supervised opponent the paper has never had on bAbI -- prompting is unsupervised and the
                     linear probe is weak, so without this the handover's margin is not attributable to structure.
  lora_through_vsa   LoRA fine-tuned with the loss taken AFTER bind, bundle, unbind and cleanup, gradients
                     flowing through the algebra and into the model. Symbol codes come from a projection of span
                     states learned jointly; NO identity labels are supplied, because the point is whether the
                     model can learn a bindable code on its own.
  Banked references, not recomputed: handover 1.000 / 1.000, prompting .792 / .386, last-token probe .771 / .245.

**Bars.**
(a) TRAINING THROUGH THE VSA WORKS iff lora_through_vsa >= 0.95 on task 1 AND >= 0.95 on task 2, in 3/3. Then the
    paper's central negative claim is wrong as stated for a trainable encoder, the abstract sentence "a projection
    trained through the loss never works" must be rewritten to say "never works with the encoder frozen", and
    this becomes the paper's main positive result rather than its main negative.
(b) IT STILL FAILS WITH A TRAINABLE ENCODER iff lora_through_vsa <= lora_direct - 0.05 in 3/3 on BOTH tasks. Then
    the negative generalises from frozen to trainable and the paper says so, which strengthens it.
(c) GRADED otherwise: report and license neither.
(d) SEPARATELY, the control the paper needs regardless: THE HANDOVER SURVIVES A SUPERVISED OPPONENT iff
    1.000 - lora_direct >= 0.10 on task 2 in 3/3. If lora_direct reaches the handover, then the fifty-eight point
    margin over prompting was about supervision and not about structure, and the capability claim comes out.

**Predictions on the record, and the honest uncertainty.** I expect lora_direct near .95 on task 1 -- one hop, and
prompting is already .792 -- and somewhere between .5 and .8 on task 2, so (d) holds but by less than the margin
over prompting suggests. I expect (b) rather than (a), because credit assignment through a cleanup arg-max is
brutal and 775-900 instances is little data for it. But I want to state plainly that I cannot rule out (a): with
the encoder trainable the model can move symbols into positions that bind, which is a mechanism the frozen
experiments could not test, and every previous negative in this family was measured with that door shut. Thirty
predictions tested today and twenty-one failed, so the prediction is worth the bar and no more.

**What I will not do.** If (a) comes out I will not keep the frozen-encoder negative as the headline; and if (d)
fails I will not keep the fifty-eight point comparison against prompting as a capability claim.

## V-50: the supervised opponent, and the trainable encoder. One capability claim earned, one killed, and the
## objection about training through the VSA is half right.

**Task 1 (one hop, all lengths).**
  handover (banked)   1.0000
  lora_direct         [.998 1.000 1.000]  0.9993
  prompting (V-49)    0.7920      last-token probe  0.7713
Bar (d) requires handover - lora_direct >= 0.10 in 3/3; it is .0007. **THE HANDOVER DOES NOT SURVIVE A SUPERVISED
OPPONENT ON TASK 1.** Per the prereg, the twenty-one point margin over prompting was about SUPERVISION and not
about structure, and the task-1 capability claim comes out. That also retires V-49's task-1 verdict, which held
by eight thousandths and is now moot: a LoRA fine-tune with no VSA anywhere reaches the same 1.000.

**Task 2 (two hops, expressible subset, 775 train / 420 eval).**
  handover (banked)      1.0000
  lora_direct            [.8500 .6952 .8571]  0.8008
  lora_through_vsa       [.5643 .6190 .6167]  0.6000     trainable encoder, NO identity labels
  frozen spans (V-37b)   [.4952 .5048 .5071]  0.5024     frozen encoder, NO identity labels
  prompting (V-49)       0.3860               last-token probe  0.2452
Bar (d): 1.000 - lora_direct = .150 / .3048 / .1429, all >= .10. **THE HANDOVER SURVIVES A SUPERVISED OPPONENT ON
TASK 2.** Structure is worth about twenty points over a fine-tune trained on the same labels and the same
instances, in three of three seeds. This is the paper's capability claim and it is a two-hop claim.

**The objection was half right, and the half that is right is measurable.** Unfreezing the encoder moves the
through-VSA route from .5024 to .6000 on the identical task, subset and label budget -- about ten points. So the
frozen encoder WAS handicapping it and every previous negative in this family was measured with that door shut.
The objection is wrong about the conclusion: at .6000 the route is still twenty points below a plain LoRA
fine-tune with no VSA at all (.8008) and forty below the discrete handover (1.0000). Bar (b) holds in 3/3.

**So the paper's central negative narrows rather than falls.** Not "a projection trained through the loss never
works" but: with the encoder frozen it stays at or below the floor; with the encoder trainable it improves by
about ten points and still loses to both a plain fine-tune and the discrete handover. The abstract sentence must
be rewritten to say that, and the improvement must be reported, not omitted.

**Coherent picture across the two tasks, and it matches V-48's mechanism.** One hop: the model already does it
(.792 zero-shot), fine-tuning finishes it (.9993), the algebra adds nothing. Two hops: the model cannot (.386),
fine-tuning gets partway (.8008), and the algebra with a discrete identity handover is exact (1.0000). V-48
showed the final-position state bridges one hop and not two, which is exactly where structure starts to pay.

**Limits to state in the manuscript, not in a footnote.** LoRA is r=8, two epochs, 775 instances; a longer or
larger fine-tune may close part of the twenty points, and the seed spread (.695 to .857) is wide. The handover
uses identity labels the fine-tune does not; the fine-tune uses only the answer label. So the comparison is
"structure plus identity supervision" against "answer supervision alone", which is the honest framing and is how
the sentence will read.

**Apparatus, disclosed above and repeated here.** The task-1 through-VSA arm was VOID on the first attempt
because I compared an offset location id against an unoffset label; it scored .08 identically across seeds with a
falling loss, which is a bug signature. Fixed, and a guard now ABORTS any run where more than half of the
training rows have the label outside the candidate list. Task 2 reported 0 of 775 rows skipped, so its numbers
are clean by that check.

**Tally.** Thirty-two predictions tested today, twenty-two failed. I predicted lora_direct near .95 on task 1
(.9993, right), .5 to .8 on task 2 (.8008, right at the top of the range), and bar (b) rather than (a) (right).

## V-51 prereg: screen for where the model FAILS, before choosing where to apply structure. Before any code.

**The one regularity that survived today.** Structure pays where the model's own mechanism fails, and nowhere
else: at one hop the model is at .792 and a plain fine-tune reaches .999, so the algebra adds nothing; at two hops
the model is at .386 and the fine-tune stops at .801, so the handover's 1.000 is worth twenty points. V-48 gives
the mechanism -- the final-position state bridges one hop and not two. So the way to find further gains is not to
guess a task but to MEASURE where the model fails and then ask which of those failures the algebra can express.

**Screen.** Prompting only, no training: zero-shot and four-shot on bAbI tasks 1 through 20, next-token
distribution restricted to that task's own answer set, three prompt draws. Cheap, and it produces the candidate
list rather than letting me choose one.

**The expressibility taxonomy is fixed HERE, before any number is seen.** A task is EXPRESSIBLE iff its answer
can be obtained by unbinding a key from a bundle of role-filler pairs, with at most an ordering rule supplied
from outside the algebra (as used on tasks 1 and 2). By that definition, and committed now:
  EXPRESSIBLE: 1, 2, 11, 12, 13 (single and compound coreference are bundles of entities), 4, 5, 15, 16
  NOT EXPRESSIBLE: 3 (asks "before", a temporal order a superposition cannot hold), 6/9/10 (yes/no and
    indefinite knowledge -- the answer is not an entity retrieved by unbinding), 7 (counting), 8 (lists, the
    answer is a set with cardinality), 14 (temporal), 17/18/19 (positional and path reasoning over relations we
    do not encode), 20 (motivation, not retrieval)
Any task I later want to move between these lists must be moved in a new ledger entry with a reason, not
silently.

**Bars.**
(a) A task is a CANDIDATE iff it is EXPRESSIBLE by the list above AND the better prompting arm is <= 0.60 in 3/3
    draws. Both conditions, and the expressibility half was fixed before the numbers.
(b) THE SEARCH SUCCEEDS iff at least one task other than 2 is a candidate. Those tasks then get the full arm set
    -- handover, lora_direct, prompting -- in V-52, and any gain is reported against a supervised opponent as on
    task 2, never against prompting alone.
(c) THE SEARCH FAILS iff task 2 is the only candidate. Then the twenty-point gain is a single-task result, the
    paper says so, and I stop looking for more of them on bAbI rather than widening the taxonomy until something
    qualifies.

**Predictions on the record.** I expect tasks 2 and 16 to be candidates, and I expect 11 and 13 NOT to be --
coreference here is two sentences long and a 2.7B model resolves it. I also expect several NOT EXPRESSIBLE tasks
to score badly, which is exactly why the taxonomy had to be fixed first: a low number on task 3 or 7 is not an
opportunity for this algebra. Thirty-two predictions tested today and twenty-two failed.

**What I will not do.** I will not move a task into EXPRESSIBLE because it turned out to be hard, and I will not
report a prompting-only gap as a capability result. Task 2's twenty points exist because a supervised fine-tune
was measured on the same data; anything found here gets the same opponent or it does not get claimed.

the argument for screening rather than choosing: had I picked by hand I would have run 16 and missed both new

called opportunities -- 3 at .2733, 14 at .4778, 17 at .5189 -- and all three are inexpressible for reasons fixed
in the prereg before any number existed: "before" is a temporal order a superposition cannot hold, task 14 is
temporal, task 17 is positional relations we do not encode. Without the taxonomy fixed first, task 3's .2733
would have looked like the best opportunity on the board.

## V-52 prereg: the two new candidates, with the supervised opponent and a memorisability check. Before any code.

**What is being tested.** V-51's screen produced candidates 2, 4 and 15 from a taxonomy fixed before any number
was seen. Task 2 already has its full arm set. This entry gives tasks 4 and 15 the same treatment: handover,
lora_direct, prompting, and the through-loss projection, so any gain is measured against an opponent trained on
the same instances with the same answer labels -- never against prompting alone.

**Structures, with the outside rules named.**
  Task 15 (entity to class to property): membership statements bind class to entity, class statements bind
    property to class; the query unbinds the entity to get a class, cleans up against the classes present, then
    unbinds the class to get the property. Two genuine hops. Plural and singular mentions of one animal -- "Mice"
    and "mouse" -- must map to the SAME symbol, which is a mention partition the identity head has to learn.
    No outside rule is needed.
  Task 4 (two-argument relational lookup): each statement "A is DIR of B" is stored twice, as A keyed by
    (DIR, B) and as B keyed by (inverse(DIR), A), because the questions come in both directions. The inverse
    mapping north/south and east/west is SUPPLIED FROM OUTSIDE the algebra, exactly as the ordering rule is on
    tasks 1 and 2, and the manuscript must say so in the same sentence as any result.

**The memorisability check, which comes FIRST and can void a task outright.** The four task-15 instances I
inspected carry identical statements, so the knowledge base may be constant across the corpus. If it is, a
fine-tune can simply memorise "gertrude -> wolf" while prompting fails only because it was never told the
knowledge base, and any margin would be an artifact of who saw the corpus rather than of structure. So, before
any arm runs: count the distinct answer sets per query key across the training corpus.
  MEMORISABLE iff the query key determines the answer uniquely in more than 95% of training instances. A
  MEMORISABLE task is reported as such and NO capability claim is made from it, whatever the arm numbers say.
This applies to task 4 as well.

**Bars, per task, only for tasks that are not memorisable.**
(a) ADMISSION: parser - prompting >= 0.20, else void for lack of room.
(b) STRUCTURE PAYS iff handover - lora_direct >= 0.10 in 3/3 seeds.
(c) NO GAIN iff handover - lora_direct <= 0.02 in 3/3.
(d) GRADED otherwise.
Reported alongside without bars: the through-loss projection, and the label asymmetry -- the handover is given
identity labels the fine-tune is not, so every comparison reads "structure plus identity supervision against
answer supervision alone", as on task 2.

**Predictions on the record.** Task 15 is MEMORISABLE and will be voided -- the statements repeat verbatim, so
lora_direct should approach 1.0 by memorising the knowledge base. Task 4 is not memorisable, because the room
pairs differ per instance, and there I expect STRUCTURE PAYS, since the failure is a relation-inversion error
and the algebra is given the inverse rule while the fine-tune must learn it. Thirty-three predictions tested
today and twenty-three failed.

**What I will not do.** I will not report a margin over prompting as a gain on a memorisable task, and I will not
drop the memorisability check if it voids the task I would rather keep.

## V-52 NO GAIN on task 15 -- and it corrects the condition under which structure pays

**Numbers (bAbI task 15, 4 animals, 4 entity names, codebook 8, 900 train / 500 eval, 3 seeds).**
  lora_direct    [.992 .992 .990]  0.9913
  parser         [.824 .848 .836]  0.8360      exact codes, learns nothing
  probe_argmax   [.824 .848 .836]  0.8360      identical to parser, per seed
  spans          [.462 .470 .492]  0.4747      at the floor, as in every synthetic arena
  floor          [.442 .510 .468]  0.4733      last-token probe, the paper's convention
  prompting      0.3867 (banked, V-51)
Admission passes (parser - prompting = .4493). Verdict NO GAIN by bar (c), and the accurate statement is stronger
than the bar's wording: the fine-tune BEATS the handover by .168, .144 and .154, in three of three seeds.

**The ceiling is the algebra's, not the handover's.** probe_argmax equals parser to the seed, so identity is not
the limitation -- the supervised head is already reproducing exact codebook rows. The parser itself stops at
.8360, which means about one instance in six cannot be expressed by this bundle at all. Where the algebra is not
exact, a supervised fine-tune goes past it.

**Which corrects the condition I had been reading off task 2.** Two hops is NOT the condition.
  task 2   object -> holder -> location   parser and handover exact at 1.000   structure +20 over lora_direct
  task 15  entity -> class -> property    parser and handover cap at .836      structure -15 against lora_direct
The condition is that the ALGEBRA MUST BE EXACT on the task. Where it is, the handover inherits that exactness
and beats a fine-tune; where it is not, the fine-tune passes it. Task 2's twenty points are therefore a
conditional result and the manuscript must state the condition, not the hop count.

**My prediction was wrong twice over on this task.** I predicted task 15 would be MEMORISABLE (it is not: 225
distinct statement blocks, key->answer unique in 0.0000) and, having been cleared, that it would be a candidate
worth the arm set -- which it was, and the arms said no. Thirty-five predictions tested today, twenty-four
failed.

**A hypothesis for the .836, registered as a hypothesis and not asserted.** In this task a class can appear both
as a key and as a value inside one bundle -- "Wolves are afraid of cats" makes wolf a key while "Mice are afraid
of wolves" makes wolf a value -- and binding one symbol into a bundle in both roles creates interference that
HRR's cleanup cannot always resolve. Task 2 has no such reuse: objects, holders and locations are disjoint sets.
That is testable by measuring accuracy split on whether the queried chain touches a reused symbol, and it is
registered next as V-53 rather than written into the paper now.

**What goes in the manuscript.** The task-15 numbers, the statement that the fine-tune wins there, and the
corrected condition. Not a hop-count story.

## V-53 prereg: why the algebra caps at .836 on task 15. Before any code.

**What needs explaining.** V-52 showed the parser -- exact codes, no learning -- stops at .8360 on task 15 while
reaching 1.000 on task 2, and that this ceiling, not the handover, is what lets a fine-tune win there. The
manuscript now rests on the condition "structure pays where the algebra is exact", so the reason the algebra is
inexact here is load-bearing and must be measured rather than asserted.

**The hypothesis.** In task 15 one animal can occupy both roles inside a single instance: "Wolves are afraid of
cats" makes wolf a KEY, "Mice are afraid of wolves" makes wolf a VALUE, and both bindings sit in the same bundle.
HRR's cleanup has to separate a symbol from itself in a different role. Task 2 has no such reuse -- objects,
holders and locations are disjoint vocabularies -- which would explain why it is exact.

**Measurement.** Parser arm only, no training, same instances and seeds as V-52. For each evaluation instance,
mark it REUSED iff the queried chain's class or its property also appears in the other role somewhere in that
instance's class statements. Split parser accuracy on that flag and report both subsets with their sizes.

**Bars.**
(a) REUSE EXPLAINS IT iff parser accuracy on NOT-REUSED >= 0.95 in 3/3 AND on REUSED <= 0.70 in 3/3. Then the
    manuscript can state the mechanism: the bundle fails when a symbol is bound in two roles at once, and the
    task-2 versus task-15 difference is role disjointness.
(b) NOT REUSE iff the two subsets are within 0.05 of each other in 3/3. Then my hypothesis is wrong, the .836 has
    another cause, and the manuscript reports the ceiling without explaining it.
(c) GRADED otherwise: report both subsets and claim no mechanism.
Void condition: if either subset has fewer than 50 instances the split is not readable and I say so.

**Prediction.** (a). The mechanism is concrete and the arithmetic of HRR makes it plausible: unbinding a key that
is also present as a value returns a superposition of the intended value and whatever that key was bound to as a
value. Thirty-five predictions tested today and twenty-four failed, and I note that this is the second
mechanism-shaped prediction I have made tonight after V-48's, which held.

**What this does either way.** Under (a) the paper gains a stated condition with a mechanism behind it -- role
disjointness -- which is checkable by a reader against any new task before they try the algebra on it. Under (b)
the paper keeps the ceiling as an unexplained limit, which is weaker but still corrects the hop-count reading.

## V-53 VOID: the contrast group does not exist inside task 15

All 500 evaluation instances came out REUSED, so the split has no comparison group and the registered void
condition (either subset under 50) fired. That is a fact about the task rather than a failure of the diagnostic:
task 15's class statements always form a cycle over four animals -- keys {mice, cats, sheep, wolves} against
values {wolves, sheep, wolves, cats} -- so the key and value sets always intersect and the queried chain almost
always touches the intersection. There is no disjoint-role subset to compare against.

The hypothesis is not refuted; it is untestable this way. It must be tested by CONSTRUCTING the contrast rather
than looking for it, and since it concerns HRR's cleanup rather than any language model, it can be tested in the
algebra alone.

## V-54 prereg: does binding one symbol in two roles degrade HRR retrieval? Before any code, no LLM involved.

**Why in the algebra alone.** The claim under test -- that a bundle degrades when a symbol appears as both key
and value -- is a property of circular convolution and cleanup, not of Phi-2. Testing it with an encoder in the
loop would add two confounds (code quality and span selection) to a question that has neither. So this runs on
random unit hypervectors with no model at all, which also makes it exactly reproducible.

**Setup.** HRR at the paper's dimension, $d = 2048$, circular convolution for binding and correlation for
unbinding, near-orthogonal random codebooks, cleanup by cosine against the candidate set -- the same primitives
v13 uses. Two-hop retrieval: bundle 1 maps entities to classes, bundle 2 maps classes to properties, query an
entity and retrieve its property through a cleanup between the hops, exactly the task-15 structure.
Conditions, each at $N$ = 4, 8, 16, 32 bindings per bundle and 2000 trials per cell, seeds 0/1/2:
  DISJOINT   the key vocabulary and the value vocabulary of bundle 2 share no symbol
  SHARED     the two vocabularies are the same set, so a symbol can be a key and a value at once
Nothing else differs -- same dimension, same number of bindings, same candidate-set size at cleanup.

**Bars.**
(a) ROLE REUSE DEGRADES RETRIEVAL iff DISJOINT - SHARED >= 0.10 at some tested $N$, in 3/3 seeds, AND the gap is
    monotone non-decreasing in $N$ across the tested values. Then the paper may state role disjointness as the
    condition behind task 2 versus task 15, with a measured mechanism.
(b) NO EFFECT iff |DISJOINT - SHARED| <= 0.02 at every tested $N$ in 3/3. Then reuse is not the mechanism, the
    task-15 ceiling stays unexplained in the paper, and I say the hypothesis was tested and refuted.
(c) GRADED otherwise: report the table and claim no mechanism.

**Prediction.** (a), with the gap widening in $N$. Unbinding a key that is also present as a value returns the
intended value plus a cross-term, and the number of cross-terms grows with the number of bindings. Thirty-six
predictions tested today and twenty-five failed; this is the third mechanism-shaped one and the previous two --
V-48's one-hop shortcut and V-52's exactness condition -- both held.

**Honest limit, stated now.** Even under (a) this is a statement about HRR at $d = 2048$ with random codebooks,
not about task 15 specifically. It would explain the ceiling; it would not prove that reuse is the whole of it.
The manuscript must say "consistent with" rather than "because of" unless the task-15 numbers are recovered by a
simulation matched to its exact structure, which this run does not attempt.

## V-54 GRADED -- stopped by a bar I mis-specified, with the effect itself unambiguous

**Numbers (pure HRR, d = 2048, no model, 2000 trials per cell, seeds 0/1/2).**
  N     DISJOINT              SHARED                gap per seed
  4     [1.0 1.0 1.0] 1.0000  [.528 .4825 .4755] .4953  [.472 .5175 .5245]
  8     [1.0 1.0 1.0] 1.0000  [.5065 .5025 .504] .5043  [.4935 .4975 .496]
  16    [1.0 1.0 1.0] 1.0000  [.503 .500 .492]   .4983  [.497 .500 .508]
  32    [1.0 1.0 1.0] 1.0000  [.4825 .500 .517]  .4998  [.5175 .500 .483]
A gap of at least .10 in three of three seeds at EVERY tested N -- twelve cells, no exception -- and disjoint
retrieval is exactly 1.0000 in all twelve.

**Verdict GRADED, by my own bar, and I am not relabelling it.** Bar (a) required the gap to be monotone
non-decreasing in N as well as large. It is flat: .5047, .4957, .5017, .5002. So the registered verdict is GRADED
and the manuscript may not cite this as a bar-licensed mechanism.

**The monotonicity requirement was wrong-headed, and the reason is the mechanism itself.** I added it expecting
cross-terms to accumulate with the number of bindings. They do not. There is ONE dominant cross-term: convolution
commutes, so unbinding mem2 by cls[c] returns cls[c+1] as intended AND, because c is also the value bound to
c-1, returns cls[c-1] essentially cleanly. Two clean candidates, one cleanup, fifty per cent -- which is exactly
what the numbers show and why the gap does not grow with N. I wrote an incorrect mechanistic intuition into a
bar and the bar then blocked the correct conclusion. That is the bar working as designed on a badly designed bar.

**The disciplined repair is not to widen the bar after the fact.** It is to register the corrected bar and rerun
on fresh seeds, so the conclusion is licensed by a prediction rather than by hindsight. Registered immediately
below.

## V-55 prereg: the same test with the bar corrected and fresh seeds. Before the rerun.

**What changes.** Only the bar and the seeds. The experiment, dimension, trial count and conditions are V-54's
verbatim; seeds become 10/11/12 so the numbers are new data and not a rescoring of V-54's.

**Corrected bars.**
(a) ROLE REUSE DEGRADES RETRIEVAL iff DISJOINT - SHARED >= 0.10 at EVERY tested N, in 3/3 seeds. No monotonicity
    requirement: the mechanism predicts a constant gap, not a growing one, and the bar now says what the
    mechanism says.
(b) NO EFFECT iff |DISJOINT - SHARED| <= 0.02 at every tested N in 3/3.
(c) GRADED otherwise.
Registered additionally, as the mechanism's own signature: SHARED accuracy should sit near 0.50 -- two clean
candidates and one cleanup -- and I will report it as consistent only if every SHARED cell falls in [0.40, 0.60].
If SHARED comes in far from .50 the two-clean-candidate account is wrong even if the gap is large.

**Prediction.** (a), with every SHARED cell inside [0.40, 0.60]. Thirty-seven predictions tested today and
twenty-five failed.

**The limit stays as registered at 8f3daa3.** Even under (a) this is HRR at d = 2048 with random codebooks, so the
manuscript says role reuse is consistent with the task-15 ceiling, not that it is the whole cause.

## V-55 ROLE REUSE DEGRADES RETRIEVAL, and the mechanism signature holds

**Numbers (pure HRR, d = 2048, no model, 2000 trials per cell, fresh seeds 10/11/12, scored by score55.py which
did not run the experiment).**
  N     DISJOINT   SHARED per seed              gap per seed
  4     1.0000     [.501 .493 .503]  .4990     [.499 .507 .497]
  8     1.0000     [.4965 .480 .5035] .4933    [.5035 .520 .4965]
  16    1.0000     [.4945 .5055 .504] .5013    [.5055 .4945 .496]
  32    1.0000     [.505 .509 .5065]  .5068    [.495 .491 .4935]

**Both registered conditions hold.** The gap is at least .10 at every tested N in three of three seeds -- in fact
about .50 everywhere -- and the mechanism signature holds too: every SHARED cell falls inside [0.40, 0.60], which
is what two clean candidates and one cleanup predicts. Disjoint retrieval is exactly 1.0000 in all twelve cells.
The gap is flat in N, as the single-dominant-cross-term account requires and as V-54's mis-specified monotonicity
bar wrongly forbade.

**What this licenses, and in what words.** Role disjointness is the condition, and the mechanism is stated: since
circular convolution commutes, unbinding a bundle by a key that also appears as a VALUE elsewhere in that bundle
returns the intended value plus a second, equally clean candidate -- the item that key was bound to as a value --
and a single cleanup then picks between two clean options. The manuscript may say this is CONSISTENT WITH the
task-15 ceiling, per the limit registered at 8f3daa3, not that it is the whole cause: this is HRR at d = 2048
with random codebooks, not a simulation matched to task 15's exact statement graph.

**The line this closes.** V-49 and V-50 established that structure is worth twenty points on task 2 against a
fine-tune with the same labels and nothing at all on task 1. V-51 screened all twenty bAbI tasks with a taxonomy
fixed before the numbers and produced candidates 2, 4 and 15. V-52 ran task 15 and structure LOST by fifteen
points, because the algebra itself caps at .836 there. V-53 tried to explain that inside task 15 and voided
because every instance is reused. V-54 moved the question into the algebra and was blocked by my own bad bar.
V-55 answers it. So the condition under which VSA helps a language model, as measured tonight, is:
  the model's own single-pass mechanism must fail on the task -- one hop it does not, two hops it does -- AND
  the relation's key and value vocabularies must be disjoint, or the algebra caps below what a fine-tune reaches.
Both halves are measured, the second is a property of HRR rather than of any model, and a reader can check both
on a new task before spending anything.

**Tally.** Thirty-seven predictions tested today, twenty-five failed. Nine apparatus or specification faults
disclosed, including two mis-specified bars of my own (V-21's and V-54's) and two duplicate launches.

## V-56 prereg: use the condition to PREDICT, and test whether the gain scales. Before any code.

**Why these two.** V-55 licensed a two-part condition: structure pays when the model's own single pass fails AND
the relation's key and value vocabularies are disjoint. A condition that only describes what already happened is
worth little. Part A turns it into a prediction that can fail. Part B asks whether, where the condition holds, the
gain grows with the number of hops -- which is the difference between a narrow result and a scaling one.

**Part A: task 4, predicted to FAIL by my own condition.** In bAbI task 4 every argument of the relation is a
room: "The office is north of the kitchen" makes office a value and kitchen part of the key, and elsewhere kitchen
is a value. Key and value vocabularies are the SAME set, so V-55 says the bundle should cap. Prompting is .4411,
so the model does fail there and the first half of the condition holds; the second half does not. Arms: floor,
parser, probe_argmax, spans, lora_direct, exactly as on task 15. The inverse relation (north/south, east/west) is
supplied from outside the algebra, and -- registered here as an amendment, because it is a real weakening -- the
four direction words are given CODEBOOK ROWS rather than codes derived from states, since after inversion a
direction may have no mention in the text. Rooms still come from span states via the handover. Any task-4 result
is therefore a hybrid and the manuscript must say so.
  CONDITION PREDICTS CORRECTLY iff parser <= 0.90 AND lora_direct - probe_argmax >= 0.05, in 3/3 seeds. The
  algebra caps and the fine-tune passes it, as reuse predicts.
  CONDITION FAILS iff probe_argmax - lora_direct >= 0.10 in 3/3. Structure would then win on a reused-role task,
  the condition would be wrong as stated, and I would withdraw it rather than add an exception.
  GRADED otherwise.

**Part B: does the gain scale with hops where the condition holds?** Arena C, roles and fillers drawn from
disjoint vocabularies by construction, at HOPS = 1, 2, 3, with the full arm set including lora_direct fine-tuned
on the same instances. bAbI has no three-hop disjoint-role task, so this half is synthetic and the manuscript
will say that.
  THE GAIN SCALES iff (probe_argmax - lora_direct) is >= 0.10 at HOPS = 2 AND strictly larger at HOPS = 3 than at
  HOPS = 2, in 3/3 seeds.
  THE GAIN DOES NOT SCALE iff the difference at HOPS = 3 is not larger than at HOPS = 2 in 3/3.
  Admission per depth: parser - floor >= 0.20, else that depth is void.

**Predictions on the record.** Part A: CONDITION PREDICTS CORRECTLY. Part B: THE GAIN SCALES, because the model's
single pass degrades with hops while the algebra with disjoint roles does not until capacity runs out, and V-43
put that capacity limit at four hops, not three. Thirty-seven predictions tested today and twenty-five failed.

**What I will not do.** If Part A comes out CONDITION FAILS I will withdraw the two-part condition rather than
patch it with an exception for task 4. If Part B does not scale, the twenty points stays a single-depth result and
the manuscript says the gain does not grow.

## V-56 AMENDMENT, registered before Part B runs: my own condition is refuted by data already in this paper

**What I got wrong, and it is in the manuscript as of twenty minutes ago.** I wrote that the relation's key and
value vocabularies must be DISJOINT. Arena C, which has been in this paper all along, draws roles and fillers from
the SAME vocabulary -- v13's generator takes both from range(N_SYM) -- and its parser arm reaches .934 to 1.000.
By the coarse condition it should have collapsed to one half. It does not. So the coarse condition is false, and
it is false against evidence I already had, which I should have checked before writing it.

**The refinement, which explains four datasets rather than two.** V-55's collapse needs the spurious cross-term to
be a candidate at cleanup. Unbinding a bundle by key k returns the intended value plus, cleanly, whatever item k
was bound to as a value elsewhere -- but that item only wins if the cleanup is allowed to choose it. So:
  COLLAPSE HAPPENS iff the cleanup candidate set CONTAINS the spurious item.
  V-55 SHARED: candidates are the whole shared pool, the spurious item is in it -> .50, collapse.
  Arena C: candidates are that level's FILLERS while the spurious item is a ROLE -> not in the set -> .934-1.000.
  Task 15: candidates are the animals and the spurious item is also an animal -> in the set -> .836 ceiling.
  Task 2: candidates are locations while the spurious item is an object or a person -> not in the set -> 1.000.
The operative property is therefore the CANDIDATE SET, not the vocabulary. Disjoint vocabularies are one way to
get it; a candidate set restricted to one role's inventory is another, and is what arena C and task 2 have.

**Consequences I am committing to now.**
1. The manuscript sentence stating the disjointness condition is WRONG and comes out, replaced by the candidate-set
   version, with arena C named as the case that refutes the coarse reading. This is a correction of my own text,
   not a rewording.
2. V-56 Part B changes accordingly: arena C already has a restricted candidate set, so it cannot test the
   condition by varying vocabularies. Part B keeps only its scaling question -- does the gain over lora_direct
   grow with hops -- and the condition question moves to a new cell:
   CANDIDATE-SET TEST, in the algebra alone as V-55 was: two-hop retrieval with SHARED vocabularies, cleanup
   restricted to the true value inventory versus cleanup over the whole pool. Predicted: restricted recovers
   1.000, unrestricted stays at .50. If restricted does NOT recover, the refinement is wrong too and I withdraw
   the mechanism claim entirely rather than refine it a third time.
3. Part A's prediction for task 4 is re-derived under the refinement rather than kept: in task 4 the candidate set
   is the rooms and the spurious item is also a room, so the refined condition still predicts a cap. The Part A
   bars stand unchanged.

**Prediction on the record.** The candidate-set test recovers 1.000 when restricted. Thirty-eight predictions
tested today and twenty-five failed, and this is the second time tonight that a condition of mine was refuted by
data already in the paper -- the first was the hop-count reading that task 15 killed.

## V-56b VOID BY CONSTRUCTION -- and the mechanism claim comes OUT of the manuscript anyway

**What the run showed.** RESTRICTED .5103 / .4982 against WHOLE-POOL .4873 / .4882 at N = 4 and 8 -- no recovery.
By the letter of the prereg at 0c9080f that would withdraw the mechanism claim. By inspection the run cannot
support any conclusion at all, and the reason is mine: in v56b the value inventory is `prop_of[c] = cls[(c+1)%n]`,
whose image is exactly the class set, which is also the key set. So "restrict cleanup to the items that occur as
values" restricted nothing -- the spurious item cls[c-1] is itself the value of c-2 and stays in the candidate
set. The test I built to isolate the candidate-set effect could not vary it. VOID BY CONSTRUCTION, the third such
fault tonight after V-34 and V-53.

**I am not using "the test was broken" as a reprieve.** The prereg's purpose was to forbid a third refinement
without a passing test, and there is no passing test. So the mechanism claim comes out of the manuscript now, and
what stays is the empirical pattern with the explanation labelled as unproven:

  measured, four datasets, all standing:
    V-55        shared pool, cleanup over the whole pool          .50
    V-55        disjoint vocabularies                             1.000
    arena C     overlapping vocabularies, cleanup over that level's FILLERS only        .934-1.000
    task 2      cleanup over locations, spurious item an object or person               1.000
    task 15     cleanup over animals, spurious item also an animal                      .836 ceiling
  consistent with, NOT licensed: that the ceiling appears when the spurious cross-term is a candidate at cleanup.

**What the manuscript must lose.** The sentence requiring key and value vocabularies to be DISJOINT -- already
refuted by arena C, which has overlapping vocabularies and is exact -- and the paragraph that states the
commuting-convolution account as the reason rather than as a hypothesis. The two-part checkable condition becomes
one measured half (the model's own single pass must fail, which at one hop it does not) and one open half (when
the algebra is exact and when it is not, for which we give the four measurements and no law).

**What a valid test would need, recorded so the next attempt does not repeat this.** A construction where the
items occurring as values are of a DIFFERENT type from the keys, so restricting cleanup to the value inventory
genuinely excludes the spurious item -- which is precisely the arena C and task 2 situation. Varying that inside
one generator, rather than comparing across tasks that differ in other ways, is the experiment. It is registered
nowhere yet and I am not running it in this pass.

**Tally.** Thirty-eight predictions tested today, twenty-six failed. Ten apparatus or specification faults
disclosed, three of them void-by-construction designs of mine.

## V-57 THE GAIN DOES NOT SCALE -- because the opponent is zero here, and that is the finding

**Numbers (arena C, depths 1/2/3, 3 seeds; lora_direct = LoRA r=8 on the attention projections plus the same
last-token two-way head, trained jointly on the same instances and labels).**
  depth   floor   parser   handover   lora_direct        gap (handover - lora)
  1       .5407   .9580    .9580      [.520 .522 .480] .5073   [.434 .438 .480]
  2       .5153   .9340    .9340      [.488 .540 .474] .5007   [.444 .392 .464]
  3       .5300   .8800    .8800      [.520 .520 .506] .5153   [.364 .360 .370]
Admission passes at every depth (H = .42 / .42 / .35). The handover equals the parser exactly at all three
depths. LoRA's training loss never leaves .72-.78 against a chance level of .693, and its evaluation accuracy is
chance at every depth.

**Verdict by the registered bar: THE GAIN DOES NOT SCALE.** The gap at depth 3 is not larger than at depth 2 in
any seed. I predicted it would scale; thirty-nine tested today, twenty-seven failed.

**Both halves of the honest reading, and the manuscript gets both.**
  (i) The gap is enormous and holds at every depth -- thirty-six to forty-eight points, 3/3 -- because the
      supervised opponent CANNOT LEARN this arena at all. This extends V-15's finding (LoRA at the frozen floor
      on held-out splits, 5x budget) to joint LoRA+head training at three depths: on synthetic markup the
      equal-supervision opponent is zero.
  (ii) Precisely because the opponent is zero, the scaling question DEGENERATES here: the gap's upper bound is
      the algebra's own ceiling, which decays gently with depth (.958 -> .934 -> .880, the V-14 direction), so
      the gap tracks that decay and cannot grow. "Does the gain grow with hops" is testable only where the
      opponent has real purchase -- bAbI, where LoRA reaches .999 at one hop and .801 at two -- and bAbI has no
      three-hop disjoint-role task. So the answer on natural text remains open, and the manuscript says open,
      not no.

**The complementary pair this completes.** On synthetic markup the opponent is zero and the gap is ~45 points;
on natural text the opponent is strong and the gap is 20 points at two hops and nothing at one. In every cell of
both, the handover sits exactly on the algebra's ceiling. What varies across settings is the OPPONENT, never the
handover -- which is a cleaner statement of what the discrete handover buys than any single gap number.

**External parallel, from the literature search, to enter Related Work.** PathHD (NeurIPS 2025 NORA spotlight,
arXiv 2512.09369) reports Hits@1 86.2 on WebQSP against RoG's 85.7 (+0.5) and 71.5 on CWQ against RoG's 62.6
(+8.9): the HDC advantage concentrates on the multi-hop benchmark, an independent pipeline (KG path retrieval +
one LLM call) showing the same one-hop/multi-hop gradient our controlled comparison shows (0 points at one hop,
20 at two). Attention-as-Binding (arXiv 2512.14709) supplies the shared reading: attention performs approximate,
soft unbinding, so its errors compound with hops while exact algebraic unbinding does not. Both cited as
parallels, neither as proof.

**Tally.** Thirty-nine predictions tested today, twenty-seven failed.
