## 2026-09-16 — V-137 CLOSED: frontier readers do NOT collapse at volume. V-135's +0.747 is the 32B's property, not the algebra's.

**Question, user-directed** ("我希望找到vsa胜过前沿模型的证据"). V-135 had the local Qwen2.5-32B falling
.925 → .250 between 120 and 2000 facts with zero truncation while the sharded store held .997. Does that
survive against frontier readers? Prereg `1f3d10d`, amendment `74b83b0` (both written before any API call;
the first launch made one call and died on the previous key's exhausted cap, so no data preceded the
amendment). New key supplied by the user.

**What I would not do, stated in the amendment before the data:** search configurations until one flatters
the store. What makes the question well posed is a mechanism — a sharded store's readout is set by facts
**per shard** and is flat in total volume by construction, while every reader's context is finite — so the
registerable question is whether the crossing volume sits **inside** the window the reader can read. A win
bought by overflowing the context is not a win; V-131 withdrew a 47-point separation that was exactly that.
Bars were therefore taken only on untruncated cells.

**Result. Identical instances, facts and ordering throughout; pseudo-names with no semantic handle and
three decoy relations per chain node.**

| facts | prompt tokens | store | glm-5.3 | kimi-k3 | local 32B |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 120 | 1.3k | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | 1.0000 | .9250 |
| 2000 | 21k | .9972 | .9750 | 1.0000 | **.2500** |
| 4000 | 42k | 1.0000 | .9750 | 1.0000 | — |
| 8000 | 84k | 1.0000 | .9750 | .9750 | — |

**P1 FAILS** (store − plain = +.025 at the largest untruncated K, against a +.30 bar). **P2 FAILS** (no
admitted frontier reader falls to .60 at any untruncated K ≤ 8000). **P3 HOLDS** (store 1.0000 at K=8000,
125 shards). My *amended* expectation — that a frontier cliff would appear at 4000 or 8000 — is **refuted**;
the *original* prereg expectation, that they hold, was right.

**The correction that matters most, and it went against the result the user wanted.** In the first pass
glm-5.3 read .9750 → .9000 → .7750 as K rose, which looks exactly like the frontier cliff the run was
hunting. Its API error rate rose in lockstep (.03 → .10 → .23) and errors were scored as wrong answers. A
clean re-measure (6 retries, 900 s timeout, 2 workers) completed **40/40 with zero empty responses at both
K=4000 and K=8000** and returned **.9750 at each**. The decline was entirely my instrument. Had I not
re-run it I would have reported a false positive that happened to be the evidence the user asked for.
Deepseek-v4-pro's apparent .800/.425 carried error rates of .20/.55 and is excluded by the registered
P0(b) gate for the same reason, not read as a collapse.

**gpt-5.4 excluded on the anchor, and it is not a volume effect:** .4750 at K=120 with a **zero** error
rate — it simply answers the easy cell wrong (gold `Othaneon`, answered `Corionel`). Recorded rather than
quietly dropped.

**What this settles.** V-130 measured frontier readers losing .0000 from 8 to 1024 facts and concluded the
evidence-scale advantage is a small-model finding. V-137 extends that **eight-fold**, to 8000 facts and 84k
tokens, on a harder task than V-130's (pseudo-names, decoy relations). The manuscript's existing sentence —
*"Frontier readers handed the same 1024 facts read them at 0.95–1.00 … so the margin too is the small
model's"* — is confirmed rather than contradicted, and its scope is if anything conservative.

**Consequence for V-135.** Its headline +.747 at K=2000 is a property of the **32B reader**, not of evidence
volume. V-135's own prereg pre-wrote this scope sentence before its data existed; it now binds. The volume
axis joins depth (V-133) and knowledge location (V-134): **on accuracy against a competent reader with the
evidence in context, the algebra has no usable advantage on any of the three axes tested.** What survives is
what was always true by construction — it cannot name an absent entity, and it makes no model call
(.086 s against 4–7 s and 84k tokens at the top of this ladder).

**Spend.** 741 calls, 23.9M prompt tokens across parts B and C, under the registered caps of 1,200 and 25M.
Gateway exposes no balance meter; the previous key died mid-run with a permanent 429, which is why the caps
are enforced in-process.

| depth | store | lora_weights | ctx_cot | gap = store − lora | V-134 gap (n_kb=4) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | .8422 | .9711 | .8586 | −.1289 | −.115 |
| 2 | .6734 | .7352 | .8914 | **−.0617** | +.075 |
| 3 | .5609 | .5539 | .8391 | +.0070 | +.128 |
| 4 | .4664 | .4289 | .7945 | +.0375 | +.172 |

**P1 — FAILS, and the sign flipped.** store − lora at k=2 = **−.0617, CI [−.1143, −.0096]**: with sixteen
KBs the CI is ±.05 instead of V-134's ±.16, and it excludes zero on the NEGATIVE side. The registered claim
direction is not merely unproven at power — it is contradicted: the fine-tune composes its two-hop answers
better than the store does. V-134's +.075 at k=2 was between-KB noise (its own entry recorded per-KB spread
+.288 to −.159 across four KBs); the four KBs it drew flattered the store by roughly +.13 at every depth.

**P2 — FAILS on magnitude, exactly as preregistered.** gap(4) − gap(2) = **+.0992** against V-134's +.0969 —
the slope replicates to the third decimal — with CI [+.0510, +.1474] now cleanly excluding zero and cleanly
under the +.15 bar. The prereg recorded this precise outcome in advance ("real and smaller than we
registered as interesting"), and that is the verdict: knowledge in weights loses ground to the store at
about +.05 per additional hop, monotonically (−.129/−.062/+.007/+.038), but from a level so much lower that
the store only pulls level with the fine-tune around k=3 and leads by just +.0375 at k=4.

**P3 scope, binding as ever.** ctx_cot beats the store at every depth (.8586/.8914/.8391/.7945). This run
licenses "an algebraic memory composes better per hop than the same base model with the facts in its
weights" and NOT "the algebra beats putting the evidence in the prompt" — and the per-hop claim now carries
the level caveat above.

**Consequence for the manuscript.** Any V-134-derived sentence of the form "the store overtakes the
fine-tune at depth 2 and the gap widens to +.17" is REFUTED at power and may not appear. What may appear:
(a) the fine-tune recalls the base facts better than the store stores them (.9711 vs .8422 at k=1);
(b) composition in weights degrades ~.05/hop faster than in the store, CI excluding zero — the replicated
result; (c) neither arm is competitive with evidence-in-context at any depth. The weights-vs-store axis
therefore ends the same way as depth (V-133), location (V-134) and volume (V-135/V-137): no usable accuracy
advantage for the algebra against the strongest arm, a real-but-small structural edge on a weaker arm, and
cost/latency as the surviving axis.

**Prediction ledger.** My prereg expectation for P1 was "the CI tightens around a small POSITIVE value" —
wrong again, in the now-familiar direction of overestimating the store (~11 of the last 13 directional calls
on this line). The P2 expectation was exact.

**Store dimension flat as always** (d 2048/4096/8192 at k=4: .4294/.4664/.4661).

This closes the powered replication named in V-134's own entry. V-134's artifact and verdict stand as
recorded; the two runs are to be reported side by side, with V-136 controlling wherever they disagree.
No rescue, no further arm. Zero API spend; local GPUs only, released at run end.

## 2026-09-17 — V-139 CLOSED: NOT FOUND. Holding out symbol combinations on NATURAL text does nothing to the fine-tune.

Prereg 3c19d05, runner 0c4118f, artifact `v139_logs/v139.json`. bAbI task 2 parsed into (carrier, location)
chains; parser precision-gated (every instance it keeps, its recovered location equals the gold answer).

    A  six of twenty-four combinations removed from training, evaluated only on those   1.000 / 1.000 / 1.000
    B  matched sizes (443 train / 79 eval), evaluation combinations seen in training     1.000 / 1.000 / 1.000
    gap B - A = 0.0000  ->  NOT FOUND (registered bar: >= 0.20 to count as evidence)
    P3 control passes: B is within 0.028 of the banked standard-split 0.9722, so the parsed subset is not the
    explanation.

Reading, stated against my own hope going in. The arena-C result -- a 10.5M LoRA at the frozen-probe floor on
held-out (role, filler) pairs -- does NOT transfer to this natural-text task, and the reason is visible in the
task rather than in the model: bAbI task 2 is solved by a combination-INDEPENDENT rule ("whoever took the
object, report their last location"), so a novel (carrier, location) pair changes nothing the model has to do.
Arena C has no such rule: its pairings are arbitrary and instance-specific, so the mapping must be bound and
retrieved within the instance.

What this costs us: "generalisation to symbol combinations held out of training" is NOT by itself the property
that separates the algebra from a low-rank update. The separating property is narrower -- the pairing must be
arbitrary and instance-specific, with no rule that shortcuts it. Any statement of the claim that omits that
qualifier is broader than the evidence.

What it does not cost: the arena-C measurement stands as recorded; it is the SCOPE of the generalisation that
narrows, not the number.

Registered bar was <= 0.674 for SUPPORTED; 0.2722 clears it by a wide margin. But the number to carry is not
the 70-point gap to the store -- that gap is partly the disclosed asymmetry, since the store is handed gold
triples and this arm is not. The number to carry is **+1.9 points over not fine-tuning at all**, and that one
of the three seeds (0.2300) lands BELOW the untrained single pass. Six epochs on a thousand instances does not
teach the frozen model to do the two-hop composition from raw passages; it does not reliably help at all.

statements is:
  - given structured evidence, a fine-tune matches or beats the store (1.000 vs 0.974);
  - given only the passages, a fine-tune buys almost nothing (0.272 vs 0.253).
The separating variable is whether the evidence has to be located and bound, not how hard the task is.

low-rank update cannot locate evidence among distractors is refuted at this pool size.

## V-141 — the same sweep at N=150/300/500: **VOID, harness artifact**

The N=300 run printed EM 0.0000 with training loss stuck at 4.3 (against 0.05 at N=50). That is not a task
result. `v140.py` tokenized the prompt with `truncation=True, max_length=1400`, and HF truncates from the
RIGHT, so the tail of the prompt was cut — and the tail of the prompt is the question itself. The model was
asked to answer with no question in view.

Measured with phi-2's tokenizer, a gold-triple line is ~11 tokens:

| N | prompt tokens | under the 1400 train cap | inside phi-2's 2048 window |
|---|---|---|---|
| 50 | ~602 | yes | yes |
| 150 | ~1702 | **no** | yes |
| 300 | ~3352 | **no** | **no** |
| 1024 | ~11052 | **no** | **no** |

So N=150 would have been silently truncated too, and N>=300 cannot be asked of phi-2 at all — its window is
smaller than the pool. The run was killed at ~23 min into seed 456 and nothing from it is banked. This is
the same class of confound as the phi-2 truncation artifact that cut the V-131 pooled separation from 47 to
7.7 points; it went undetected there for longer.

**Fix, committed:** `v140.py` no longer truncates. A prompt over `--max_ctx` (default 2048, phi-2's window)
aborts the run with a message naming this void.

## 2026-09-24 — V-145 CLOSED: P1 FAILS, P2 FAILS in the OPPOSITE direction to my prediction, P3 holds. The cost axis does not deliver the claim either.

Prereg `c884c50`, frozen scorer run verbatim. V-135 instances, depth 2, `N = 60`, store cost includes build
plus both hops, reader timed at batch 1.

| K | shards | store acc | store s/q | reader acc | reader s/q | ratio | prompt tok |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 120 | 2 | 1.0000 | .0183 | .9167 | 5.167 | **282.5x** | 1,369 |
| 500 | 8 | 1.0000 | .0732 | .8667 | 6.835 | 93.4x | 5,382 |
| 1000 | 16 | 1.0000 | .1484 | .7833 | 10.418 | 70.2x | 10,664 |
| 2000 | 32 | 1.0000 | .2961 | .3667 | 18.123 | **61.2x** | 21,218 |
| 4000 | 63 | 1.0000 | .5902 | window | window | --- | --- |
| 8000 | 125 | 1.0000 | 1.1636 | window | window | --- | --- |

**P0 passes** (store reproduces V-135 at both anchor volumes). **P3 HOLDS**: the store's cost exponent is
**0.992** in log-log, cleanly linear, so sharding does not make it super-linear --- the outcome I had flagged
as the one that could embarrass the claim.

**P2 FAILS, and in the direction opposite to my registered expectation.** I predicted the cost ratio would
*grow* with volume because the reader pays prefill over a growing context. It **shrinks**: 282.5x at 120
facts to 61.2x at 2000, a growth factor of 0.22 against a bar of 3. The reason is visible in the columns:
reader time grows 3.5x for a 17x increase in facts, because GPU prefill is efficient and largely parallel,
while store time grows 16x, because my shard scan is a Python loop over S shards. **Part of this is my
implementation, not the algebra** --- a batched shard scan would change the constant --- but I measured what
I built and the registered reading stands.

**P1 FAILS on the matched-accuracy clause, and the asymmetry must be stated.** At K=2000 the cost ratio is
61.2x, far past the 10x bar, but the accuracy gap is 0.633 against a tolerance of 0.05. The bar I wrote is
two-sided, and the arm that is outside it is the **store, which is better** (1.000 against .3667). A one-sided
bar would have passed. I am not rescoring against a bar I did not register; the honest statement is that
against *this* reader the arms are never accuracy-matched at any volume, so "cheaper at matched accuracy" is
not established by this run.

**Where the matched-accuracy claim does survive, as P4 descriptive and not as a bar.** V-137 measured
kimi-k3 at **.9750 on 8000 facts**, against the store's 1.000 --- a gap of .025, inside the 0.05 tolerance.
At that volume the frontier reader consumes **83,816 prompt tokens per query** and the store consumes
**zero**. That is the matched-accuracy cost comparison, in the unit the prereg named primary (tokens), and
it is descriptive because the bar was written against the local reader.

**Two structural facts that no reader size changes.** The store makes no model call, and it has no context
ceiling: the local reader's window ends at K=4000 while the store answers at 8000 in 1.16 s.

**Running tally.** V-133 depth, V-134 knowledge location, V-135/V-137 volume, V-145 cost --- five
pre-registered runs, and the only bars that hold are P3-style "the method does not degrade" bars. On
accuracy against a competent reader the algebra has no usable advantage, and the cost advantage, tested
against a matched-accuracy requirement, is not established against the reader the bar named.

V-138. That ID had already been closed on 2026-09-17 by another session, as had V-139, which I had

## V-147 — where the VSA replicator stops finding the mapping. RUN, SCORED VERBATIM, READING VOID (my scorer's fault, not the data's)

Prereg + frozen scorer committed at a9d7dc8 **before** the sweep; git log shows the ordering. Sweep ran the
full registered grid (n in {4,5,6,7,8,9,10,12} x d in {2048..65536}, 30 seeds/cell, p=0.5, planted
isomorphism, localist gold standard at every n, PYTHONHASHSEED=0, no model, no API). `v147_score.py` was run
verbatim. Artifacts: `v147_logs/v147.json`, `v147_logs/v147_trunc.json`.

**Verdict: the registered reading is VOID.** The scorer excluded all 48 VSA cells for exceeding the
registered 0.02 iteration-cap rate, and then computed P1 and P3 from those same excluded cells anyway — it
applies the exclusion to the table and to n* (P2) only. So the line it printed, "P1 HOLDS | P2 FAILS | P3
FAILS", is the output of an internally inconsistent scorer and **must not be quoted as a result**. Three
faults, all mine, all in what I committed:

1. **The exclusion rule voids the arm it was meant to protect.** Both arms test `||x_{t+1}-x_t|| < 1e-9`.
   The localist arm runs float64 and settles at a step norm ~3e-17, seven orders below the test, so it
   always registers convergence (236 iters at n=12). The VSA arm runs float32 and plateaus at ~1.5e-8, an
   order **above** the test, dipping under only by chance — hence a cap rate of 0.13–0.50 in every cell.
   The flag separates the two dtypes, not two behaviours. Measured in `tolcheck.py`, not assumed. (I first
   stated the tolerance was *unreachable* in float32; that was too strong — it is reached, 1.29e-10 on the
   seed tested. The correct statement is that it sits below the float32 iterate's noise floor, so tripping
   it is close to a coin flip.)
2. **The cap was costing nothing**, so the measurement itself is sound. Truncation control
   (`v147_trunc.py`, diagnostic, not registered) re-ran the transition cells with the cap raised ten-fold
   and recorded the readout at t = 200/1,000/4,000/10,000/40,000:

   | cell | t=200 | t=1,000 | t=4,000 | t=10,000 | t=40,000 | dead |
   |---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
   | d=4096, n=6 | 0.67 | 0.70 | 0.70 | 0.70 | 0.70 | 0/30 |
   | d=4096, n=7 | 0.17 | 0.17 | 0.17 | 0.17 | 0.17 | 0/30 |
   | d=4096, n=8 | 0.07 | 0.07 | 0.07 | 0.07 | 0.07 | 0/30 |
   | d=65536, n=6 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 1.00 | 0/30 |
   | d=65536, n=7 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0.83 | 0/30 |
   | d=65536, n=8 | 0.57 | 0.57 | 0.57 | 0.57 | 0.57 | 0/30 |

   Every t=4,000 value equals the registered sweep's value for the same cell, no run died, and a ten-fold
   budget moves nothing.
3. **The bars sit where they cannot move.** P1/P3 are anchored at "the largest n", which the grid puts deep
   in the saturated region (n=12, VSA 0.00–0.03 at every d): P1 passes trivially at a gap of +1.00, and P3
   asks dimension to recover half a gap where no dimension recovers anything. A bar that cannot fail and a
   bar that cannot pass are not bars.

**Descriptive, reported as descriptive and NOT as a bar outcome** (raw grid, exclusion ignored since the
control shows it costs nothing). Localist 0.97–1.00 at every n, 236 iters at n=12. VSA success by (d, n):

| n | loc | 2048 | 4096 | 8192 | 16384 | 32768 | 65536 |
|--:|----:|-----:|-----:|-----:|------:|------:|------:|

either way would have decided it, and the prereg said so in advance.

**Q3 FAILS at 47% against a 50% bar.** At n=8, raising d from 2048 to 65536 -- a 32-fold increase -- moves
VSA from 0.00 to 0.47, recovering just under half the gap to the localist 1.00.

**Prediction accuracy, recorded because it is the point of registering expectations separately.** The prereg
said Q1 would hold and was the weakest evidence for exactly that reason; that Q2 and Q3 would both land ON
their bars; and that Q2 was the one most likely to break. Q2 landed exactly on +2 and Q3 missed by three
points. The expectations were right about *where* the result would be decided.

**The reading, and the number worth carrying.** Dimension moves the boundary but nothing like proportionally.
Candidate mappings at the boundary, n*^2, go 25 / 25 / 36 / 36 / 36 / 49 across a 32-fold increase in d --
an exponent of **ln(49/25)/ln(32) = 0.19**. Against this project's banked storage capacity, k* = 32/64/128/256
at d = 512/1024/2048/4096, which is **linear in d**. So:

    stored facts     k*    ~ d^1.0
    held mappings    n*^2  ~ d^0.19

**Analogical mapping does not obey the storage-capacity law, and is far worse.** That is a direct, numerical
answer to the open problem Kleyko's Survey Part II sec 3.1.2.3 states qualitatively -- that holistic
transformation "was not demonstrated to be scalable to large analogical episodes". It is not, and the rate at
which dimension buys episode size is now measured. Q3's failure is the same fact from the other side:
superposition noise is part of the limit but not all of it, since 32x the dimension buys back under half.

**Scorer gap, disclosed.** `v148_score.py` has no interpretive branch for "Q1 and Q2 hold, Q3 fails", so it
printed the verdict line and the scope note with no paragraph between them. The bars and numbers it computed
are unaffected; the missing text is the reading above, written here rather than by editing a frozen file.

Attribution: the formulation is Gayler & Levy (ANALOGY-2009); the open problem is Kleyko Survey Part II sec
3.1.2.3. No new method is claimed. SCOPE: random graphs at p=0.5, not typed higher-order analogical episodes;
the classics (Water Flow--Heat Flow, Solar System--Atom) were handled by Slipchenko & Rachkovskij (2009) with
a re-representation technique this sweep does not test. Nothing here touches the language-model question.

## V-150 — cross-talk vs analogical mapping. R1 HOLDS (against my registered prediction) / R2 FAILS / R3 HOLDS

**ID COLLISION, resolved by renumbering this entry V-149 -> V-150.** Two experiments took V-149 on
2026-09-30: this one (prereg b2f1812 08:34:24, closed 3f597b0 08:38:26) and another session's
"is the store result HRR's, or the VSA family's" (prereg 4b4389d 08:41:28) -- registered three minutes
AFTER this one had already closed. The standing rule is that a new experiment never takes a used ID, so
by the letter the later registration should move. It is not the one that moved, for a stated reason: the
later entry is already referenced by two downstream commits (b06af87, 73a6c38) and by the tick state,
while this one had no downstream references, so renumbering here touches only my own record and breaks
nothing. Recorded rather than quietly reconciled.

The collision also **overwrote artifacts on disk**: v149_prereg.md, v149_score.py, v149.py, run_v149.sh
and v149_logs/v149.json in the working tree are the other session's. This entry's files were recovered
from git (b2f1812, 3f597b0) as v150_prereg.md / v150_score.py / v150.py / run_v150.sh /
v150_logs/v150.json, with V-149 -> V-150 applied mechanically to their text. The recovery was verified by
running the frozen scorer on the recovered artifact: R1 AUC 0.9243 HOLDS, R2 crossover 0.3434 FAILS,
R3 alpha 0.222 CI [0.184,0.292] HOLDS -- identical to the numbers recorded before the overwrite.

**Do not pool this with V-146.** V-146 measures analogical mapping as Kanerva-style HOLISTIC
TRANSFORMATION; this entry measures the Gayler & Levy REPLICATOR. They are different mechanisms and their
exponents and thresholds must never be averaged or quoted for one another. What the two independently
support is only the qualitative statement that the storage threshold does not transfer to mapping --
V-146 finds a mapping tolerance of 0.9409 against storage 0.0990, this entry finds a crossover of 0.3434
against storage 0.0989. Two different numbers, two different mechanisms, one shared conclusion.

Prereg + frozen scorer b2f1812, committed **before** the sweep and before any V-150 seed existed. Runner
`v150.py`, artifact `v150_logs/v150.json`. Fresh seeds 300+s. Cap rate 0.00 in every cell; nothing excluded.

Origin: the advisor's Kanerva-2009 pointer. Of its three demonstrations, Dollar of Mexico is ruled out
(Kleyko Survey Part II sec 3.1.2 deflates it as a simple proportional analogy; V-146 died testing exactly
that) and the one-shot grandmother rule needs role--filler structure our store discards. What connects is the
**cross-talk failure mode Kanerva names qualitatively and this project has measured** -- V-95's threshold
0.0989, which orders every arena row in the manuscript.

**R0 HOLDS.** Localist >= 0.97 at every n. The grid reproduces V-148 on fresh seeds: n=8,d=4096 gives 0.07
with CI [0.00, 0.17] containing V-148's 0.00; n=8,d=65536 gives 0.57 with CI [0.40, 0.73] containing 0.47.

**R1 HOLDS, AUC 0.9243 over 1,440 runs.** `Lambda = n^2 * tau` does order the mapping grid, at the
manuscript's own arena bar of 0.90. `tau` was measured, not assumed: 0.00308 at d=65536 against the
theoretical `sqrt(2/(pi d)) = 0.0031`.

**I registered that R1 would FAIL, and I was wrong.** The recorded argument was that `Lambda` takes 0.552 at
d=2048 and 0.191 at d=65536 along the boundary -- a threefold move along the line it is supposed to mark --
and therefore could not reach AUC 0.90. **That argument conflates two different properties.** Being constant
along the boundary and ranking well over the grid are not the same thing: AUC pooled across the whole grid is
dominated by the many cells far from the boundary, where `Lambda` separates success from failure easily. A
quantity can rank 0.92 and still fail to mark the boundary. **Lesson to carry: never predict a pooled ranking
statistic from an argument about behaviour at the decision boundary, and never read a high pooled AUC as
evidence that a quantity governs the boundary.** The bars that actually test the boundary are R2 and R3, and
both say no.

**R2 FAILS, decisively and informatively.** The success/failure crossover sits at `Lambda = 0.3434`, against
the registered band [0.0791, 0.1187] around storage's 0.0989 -- **3.5x apart**. Same mechanism, different
constant. The manuscript's threshold may not be quoted for mapping, and a mapping threshold may not be quoted
for storage.

**R3 HOLDS.** Fitting `n*^2 ~ d^alpha` gives **alpha = 0.222, 95% CI [0.184, 0.292]**, excluding 0.5 on data
that did not motivate the hypothesis. `n*` by d: 5 / 5 / 6 / 6 / 7 / 7 across 2048..65536.

**The three bars together, which is the actual result.** If `Lambda` governed the boundary with a fixed
threshold, the boundary would satisfy `n^2/sqrt(d) = const`, i.e. `alpha = 0.5`. Measured `alpha` is 0.222
with a CI nowhere near it. So **cross-talk ranks the grid but does not govern it**: it is a good predictor in
bulk and the wrong law at the edge. Reference exponents for the comparison: storage capacity `k*` is linear
in d (alpha = 1.0); accumulated cross-talk predicts 0.5; analogical mapping measures 0.22.

**R4 descriptive, a hypothesis and not a finding.** Of the invariant family fixed in the prereg,
`log(n)/log(d)` is the most constant at the boundary (CV 0.0588), with `n^2/d^0.19` next (0.0893) and the
cross-talk candidate `n^2/sqrt(d)` at 0.3346. That is consistent with `n* ~ d^0.11`: **the number of entities
that can be put in correspondence grows as a small power of dimension**, against a linear law for stored
facts. Choosing an invariant by fit and calling it a result is the fishing this project does not do, so this
is registered as a hypothesis for a later sweep, not claimed.

**What this buys the next paper.** Kleyko Survey Part II sec 3.1.2.3 states, qualitatively, that holistic
transformation "was not demonstrated to be scalable to large analogical episodes". It now has three numbers:
the boundary exponent (0.22, CI [0.18, 0.29]), the fact that it is neither the storage law nor the
cross-talk law, and the recalibrated threshold (0.343 vs 0.0989). It also bounds a claim of our own: the
manuscript's one-quantity instrument is **scoped to storage**, and extending it to reasoning requires a new
constant at minimum and probably a new law.

SCOPE: random graphs at p=0.5, not typed higher-order analogical episodes; the classics were handled by
Slipchenko & Rachkovskij (2009) with a re-representation technique this sweep does not test. Mechanism is
Gayler & Levy (ANALOGY-2009). No new method claimed. Nothing here enters the npj submission.

## V-149 — is the store result HRR's, or the VSA family's? P1 HOLDS / P2 FAILS (as registered) / P3 FAILS (on my instrument, not on the models)

Prereg + frozen scorer + sweep code at 4b4389d, committed **before** the sweep and before any V-149 seed
existed; `v149_score.py` run verbatim on `v149_logs/v149.json`. Open problem registered from Kleyko,
Rachkovskij, Osipov & Rahimi, *Survey Part I* (ACM CSUR 55(6), 2022) sec 4.1 — "it is not clear whether
there is one best model, which will dominate all others, or whether each model has its own applicability
scope" — the way V-147/V-148 registered Part II sec 3.1.2.3. Both surveys were the co-author's recommended
reading (2026-09-25). Four arms from Part I sec 2.3: HRR (2.3.3), MAP (2.3.7), BSC (2.3.6), FHRR (2.3.5).
**Only the four algebra functions change**; rows, gold triples, blake2b identity, 200,003-row codebook,
pooling, shard rule, cleanup-by-argmax, seeds and PYTHONHASHSEED=0 are held fixed.

**P0 gate passes on both halves, exactly.** The HRR arm reproduces V-101 (k128 0.7433 vs banked 0.7417;
k256 0.2450 vs 0.2417) and `store_rebase` to four decimals (0.9778 vs 0.9778, per-seed 0.9767/0.9833/0.9733
identical). So every difference below is the algebra and not the rewrite — which is the only reason the
rest of this entry is readable at all.

### M2, task readout (300 banked rows, d=2048, shard 64)

| arm | EM | s/query | arithmetic |
|---|---|---|---|
| FHRR | 0.9856 | 0.0006 | complex64 multiply, O(d) |
| BSC | 0.9800 | 0.0005 | uint8 XOR + popcount, O(d), **integer only** |
| MAP | 0.9789 | 0.0004 | float32 multiply-add, O(d) |
| HRR | 0.9778 | 0.0009 | float32 FFT, O(d log d) |

**P1 HOLDS, 4 of 4 at EM >= 0.90** (bar: 3 of 4). The manuscript's family-level phrase "a vector symbolic
memory" survives on this task; it is not an HRR-only result.

**P2 FAILS, and it was registered as expected to fail.** Spread FHRR - HRR = +0.0078, bootstrap CI over the
300 rows [-0.0011, +0.0178], which contains zero; the bar was >= 0.05 with the CI excluding zero. On this
task **the algebra is not a lever.**

**Why it is not a lever, which is the part worth keeping.** M2 loads each store with one row's own gold
triples, sharded at 64 — a handful of pairs against a k\* that is 128 or more for every dense arm at
d=2048. Every model is operating far below its capacity, so the task cannot discriminate between them.
This is not a null result about VSA models; it locates the null. **The 300-row task number is not evidence
about the algebra at all.** The capacity arm is where the models separate, and they separate cleanly.

### M1, capacity law (V-101 protocol verbatim, algebra swapped)

    k* = largest pool size k whose two-hop accuracy is >= 0.70

    arm     d=512  d=1024  d=2048  d=4096      alpha
    HRR        32      64     128     256      1.000
    MAP        32      64     128     128      0.700
    BSC         0      32      64     128      1.000
    FHRR       64     128     128     256      0.600

**The models are separated by a constant factor, not by a different law.** Read the ladders rather than the
exponents: HRR is 32/64/128/256; BSC is the same ladder shifted one octave down (it reaches at d=2048 what
HRR reaches at d=1024) — **binary spatter codes buy the same capacity for exactly twice the dimension**;
FHRR is the same ladder shifted one octave **up** at the low end (k\*=64 at d=512 where HRR gets 32). FHRR's
d=1024 row (0.940 / 0.938 / 0.753 / 0.245) is almost exactly HRR's d=2048 row (0.938 / 0.938 / 0.743 /
0.245): one curve, translated. MAP tracks HRR closely but not exactly: it is level with or above HRR in 11 of the 12 capacity
cells and falls 5 points below at d=4096, k=256 (0.680 vs 0.732) -- which is the one cell that sets
its ladder and its exponent.

**P3 FAILS (MAP 0.700, FHRR 0.600 outside [0.85, 1.15]) — and the failure is my instrument, not the models.**
The k grid is octave-spaced (32/64/128/256/512), so k\* can only take octave values and a single cell
crossing the 0.70 line halves it. MAP's alpha is 0.700 for one reason: its d=4096 k=256 cell is **0.680**,
1.2 points under the line, where HRR's same cell is 0.732. FHRR's alpha is 0.600 for one reason: its d=2048
k=256 cell is **0.688**, 1.2 points under. Move either cell by two points and both ladders become
32/64/128/256 and 64/128/256/512, i.e. alpha = 1.000. **All four ladders are consistent with linear-in-d;
the registered exponent bar cannot tell "sub-linear" apart from "one cell landed two points short."** I
registered a bar my grid cannot support. Recorded as FAILED per the protocol, with the reading that the
exponent is *unresolved at this resolution*, not that MAP and FHRR are sub-linear. The fix — a finer k grid,
or k\* by interpolation across the 0.70 crossing — is a follow-up, not a retroactive edit to a frozen bar.

**What the manuscript may and may not take from this.** May: "a vector symbolic memory" as a family phrase
(P1); that the capacity law's *shape* is a family property while its *constant* is model-specific, with
BSC at 1/2 and FHRR at 2x HRR's capacity per dimension; that on a task loaded below capacity the choice
among these four algebras costs under a point. May **not**: any exponent claim per model, and any statement
that the four are equivalent — they are equivalent *on this task*, which does not load them.

### P4, the integer-only corner (descriptive, no bar)

BSC reaches 0.9800 with **no multiply anywhere** — XOR to bind, popcount to compare, majority to bundle — at
0.0005 s/query against HRR's 0.9778 at 0.0009 s/query with an FFT. Yilmaz, *ArrowFlow* (arXiv 2604.04087,
the co-author's fourth recommendation) argues that integer-ordinal arithmetic is worth an accuracy cost;
on this task **the cost is not in accuracy, it is in dimension** — BSC needs 2x d for the same k\*. Nothing
here runs ArrowFlow and nothing here is a claim about it; the argument was checked on our own store instead
of imported. Separately, and **corrected in the same session that wrote it**: the first version of
this entry said MAP "dominates HRR on every axis measured" with "the same capacity ladder". That is
wrong, and the refuting number was in my own printed table — MAP k\* at d=4096 is 128 against HRR's 256,
because MAP's k=256 cell there is 0.680 against HRR's 0.732. The defensible statement is narrower:
**MAP equals HRR on task accuracy (0.9789 vs 0.9778) at half the latency and O(d) instead of O(d log d),
and matches it on capacity everywhere except the largest dimension tested, where HRR is 5 points better
in the cell that decides the ladder.** That is still a reason to consider MAP as a default; it is not
dominance. Logged as a correction rather than silently edited, because the point of this ledger is
catching these in my own text.

### Prediction accuracy, recorded because registering expectations separately is the point

- P0 pass: right.
- P1 holds: right about the bar, **wrong about the model**. I named BSC as the arm I would bet against
  clearing 0.90; it finished second at 0.9800.
- P2 fails: right, and said in advance, including the reason.
- P3: **wrong about which model deviates.** I predicted BSC would be the deviation because majority-rule
  bundling has a different capacity law; BSC is one of the two arms that came out exactly linear
  (alpha = 1.000), and the deviations are MAP and FHRR, for a threshold artifact.
- The mechanism half of the BSC prediction was right and the location was wrong: I wrote that BSC's loss
  would come from majority bundling rather than from the XOR set-cancellation that Kleyko, Gayler & Osipov
  (arXiv 2003.11458 sec IV.B) warn about. BSC's loss *is* a bundling-capacity effect — it needs 2x d — and
  it shows up in M1 only, because M2 never loads the bundle. The cancellation warning did not bite, as
  registered: our codebook rows are random and near-orthogonal, which is the condition it does not cover.

**Instrument disclosures.** MAP bundling is the unclipped sum (MAP-I), not MAP-C. BSC majority ties on an
even stack are broken by a fair coin from the run's own seeded generator, recorded rather than defaulted.
A synthetic instrument check (random vectors, no dataset, no registered seed) was run before the prereg
commit and is disclosed in that commit message: all four algebras recover 1/1 on a single bound pair and
8/8 from a bundle of eight.

**SCOPE:** one task (2WikiMultihopQA two-hop over gold triples), one identity scheme (hash to a fixed
codebook), one cleanup rule (argmax over the candidate set), four of the eleven models Part I catalogues.
The sparse families (SBDR, Sparse Block Codes) and the matrix binders (MBAT, VTB) are not tested and
nothing here speaks for them. No language model, no API, no training.

## V-146 — analogical mapping as holistic transformation, under load and under competition. P1 FAILS / P2 HOLDS / P3 FAILS

**Transcription, 2026-09-30.** This verdict was produced by the frozen `v146_score.py` on 2026-09-25 02:02
+08 and sat in `v146_logs/v146_score_output.txt` for five days without a ledger entry, while V-147/V-148/
V-149 were registered, run and closed around it. The numbers and the closing paragraph below are the
scorer's own output, reproduced rather than re-read; the two notes at the end are transcription notes and
are marked as such. Prereg + frozen scorer 17ae06a, committed before any instance existed.

Mechanism: **holistic transformation** in the sense Kanerva (2009) points at — learn a mapping vector from
correspondences and apply it to a new episode in one vector operation, no search and no training. Open
problems registered verbatim from Kleyko Survey Part II sec 3.1.2.3: (1) "not demonstrated to be scalable
to large analogical episodes"; (2) models "lack interaction and competition of consistent alternative
mappings".

    success rate, d \ n     4       8      16      32      64     128     256
    1024                1.000   1.000   1.000   1.000   0.932   0.544   0.224
    2048                1.000   1.000   1.000   1.000   1.000   0.917   0.504
    4096                1.000   1.000   1.000   1.000   1.000   0.992   0.874
    8192                1.000   1.000   1.000   1.000   1.000   1.000   0.990

**P0 gate HOLDS.** n=4, d=4096, rho=0 gives 1.0000 against a bar of 0.95.

**P1 FAILS.** n\* goes 64 at d=1024 to 256 at d=8192 — growth 4.00x against a registered bar of >= 6x.
Scorer's reading, verbatim: *"Mapping does NOT scale linearly in d, so open problem 1 closes negatively:
holistic transformation inherits a ceiling rather than buying its way out with dimension."*

**P2 HOLDS, barely, and the descriptive sweep is the part that matters.** The intended mapping is selected
0.6667 of the time against a bar of 0.60 and a chance rate of 0.50. But P4 sweeps the overlap rho between
competing mappings:

    rho = 0.00   intended selected 1.0000
    rho = 0.25   intended selected 0.5833
    rho = 0.50   intended selected 0.6667
    rho = 0.75   intended selected 0.5278

Perfect with no competitor, and **between 0.53 and 0.67 — barely off chance — at every non-zero overlap.**
This is the only measurement this project has on Survey Part II's second open problem, and it says the
competition is essentially unresolved by the algebra alone.

**P3 FAILS.** Mapping tolerance 0.9409 against retrieval's 0.0990, |diff| 0.8419 against a bar of <= 0.03.
Scorer's reading, verbatim: *"The two regimes have DIFFERENT tolerances, so storage capacity does not
predict inference capacity and the two cannot be traded against each other. Reported as the more
interesting of the two outcomes, not the disappointing one."*

**Transcription note 1 — V-146 and V-147/V-148/V-150 are DIFFERENT MECHANISMS and their exponents must
not be pooled.** V-146's `n` counts correspondence pairs in a one-shot holistic transformation (Kanerva);
V-147/V-148/V-150's `n` counts graph nodes in a Gayler & Levy replicator max-clique search. V-146 gives
n\* growing 4x over an 8x change in d (an exponent near 0.67 in n\*); V-148/V-150 give n\*^2 ~ d^0.19-0.22
(an exponent near 0.1 in n\*). Those are not in conflict — they are two different algorithms for
"analogical mapping" — but a reader who sees both numbers in one paper will assume they are, so any write-up
must name the mechanism beside every exponent.

**Transcription note 2 — P3 here and R2 in V-150 agree in direction and differ in magnitude.** V-146:
mapping tolerance 0.9409 vs storage 0.0990. V-150: mapping crossover Lambda 0.3434 vs storage 0.0989,
3.5x apart. Both say the manuscript's storage threshold does not transfer to mapping, which is the claim
that matters and which is now supported twice on two mechanisms. The two mapping numbers are different
quantities measured on different dynamics and are not a replication of each other; reconciling them is
open.

SCOPE: synthetic correspondence sets, not typed higher-order analogical episodes; the classics (Water
Flow--Heat Flow, Solar System--Atom) were handled by Slipchenko & Rachkovskij (2009) with a
re-representation technique this sweep does not test. No new method claimed. Nothing here enters the npj
submission.

## V-151 — the capacity exponent at a resolution that can resolve it. S1 FAILS / S2 HOLDS / S3 FAILS — and S1's failure overturns V-149's own self-correction

Prereg + frozen scorer 2e29e35, committed **before** the sweep and before any V-151 number existed. Runner
is `v149.py` **verbatim**, with only the k grid and the output path changed (`--ks 8 11 16 23 32 45 64 91
128 181 256 362 512 724 1024 --out v151_logs/v151.json`), so protocol identity is by construction rather
than by assertion. `k*` by linear interpolation of the 0.70 crossing in log k. Artifact `v151_logs/v151.json`.

**S0 HOLDS, exactly.** HRR's interpolated `k*` is 41.7 / 73.3 / 136.7 / 264.7 at d = 512/1024/2048/4096,
each inside `[v, 2v)` for V-149's banked octave value 32/64/128/256. Same measurement, finer ruler. **No cell
is censored at either end**, which was the point of extending the grid to 8 and 1024.

    interpolated k*      d=512    d=1024   d=2048   d=4096     alpha        95% CI
    HRR                   41.7     73.3    136.7    264.7      0.890   [0.815, 0.953]
    MAP                   43.5     79.5    139.1    247.9      0.834   [0.807, 0.868]
    BSC                   29.3     54.3     96.0    177.1      0.861   [0.821, 0.891]
    FHRR                  79.7    139.7    249.9    456.9      0.840   [0.810, 0.870]

**S1 FAILS, for all four models, and this is the result.** Every CI excludes 1.0. Capacity is **sub-linear
in d for every algebra tested**, HRR included --- and V-149 reported HRR's ladder as 32/64/128/256, i.e.
exactly linear, `alpha = 1.000`.

**The octave grid manufactures `alpha = 1.0` by construction.** `k*` can only take octave values, and
successive octaves differ by exactly 2, so a ladder that advances one step per doubling of d *cannot*
produce any exponent but 1.0. V-149's "all four ladders are consistent with linear-in-d" was not a
measurement; it was the grid's arithmetic. The same instrument fault that made MAP look sub-linear at 0.700
made HRR look exactly linear at 1.000, and I read the first as an artifact and the second as a fact.

**My registered expectation was WRONG, in the interesting direction.** The prereg says: "S1 holds. This is
V-149's own self-correction, and the whole reason for this run is that its grid could not test it. If S1
fails for MAP or FHRR at this resolution, the sub-linearity is real and V-149's correction was itself
wrong --- which would be the more interesting outcome, and I would rather find that than confirm my own
earlier reading." It failed for all four, not just MAP or FHRR.

**S2 HOLDS, spread 0.056.** The four exponents are 0.834--0.890. So V-149's "separated by a constant factor,
not by a different law" survives, and the law is now measured: **`k* ~ d^0.85` give or take 0.03**, shared
across HRR, MAP, BSC and FHRR.

**S3 FAILS, and it is the half of V-149's constants that could never have been measured.** BSC/HRR is
0.703 / 0.741 / 0.702 / 0.669 across the four dimensions, against a registered band of [0.35, 0.65]. V-149
said "binary spatter codes buy the same capacity for **exactly twice** the dimension". At this resolution BSC
holds about **70%** of HRR's capacity at the same d, so matching HRR costs roughly **1.5x** the dimension,
not 2x. The prereg named this in advance: V-149 read "half" off a grid where one step **is** a factor of two
by construction, and the measurement could not have returned any other number.

The other half of S3 survives: FHRR/HRR at d=512 is **1.910** against a bar of >= 1.4, so "FHRR is an octave
up at the low end" is close to right.

**Consequence for the manuscript: confirmed, not contradicted, and now quantified.** The paper already says,
of raising the dimension, "The scaling is **slightly sublinear**: holding the facts-to-dimension ratio
constant, the readout drifts down from 0.844 to 0.603, because a cleanup choosing among more candidates needs
more signal than a fixed threshold allows." V-151 confirms that qualitative statement and attaches a number
to it, `alpha = 0.890`, CI [0.815, 0.953] for HRR. Two numbers in that passage are octave-quantized and the
interpolated values are 41.7 and 264.7 rather than 32 and 256; whether to quote the finer values is an
editorial call, not an error in the paper.

**Two corrections to our own closed entries, logged rather than silently edited.**
1. **V-149**: "All four ladders are consistent with linear-in-d" and "binary spatter codes buy the same
   capacity for exactly twice the dimension" are both artifacts of the octave grid. The defensible
   statements are `k* ~ d^0.85 +/- 0.03` for all four, and BSC at ~1.5x the dimension. V-149's reading that
   its P3 failure was "the instrument, not the models" was half right: the instrument was at fault, and
   correcting it does not rescue linearity, it removes it everywhere.
2. **V-150**: that entry contrasts the mapping exponent against "storage capacity k* which is linear in d
   (alpha = 1.0)". The storage exponent is 0.89, not 1.0. The contrast survives easily --- 0.22 against 0.89
   is still a factor of four in the exponent --- but the number must be quoted as 0.89.

SCOPE: 2WikiMultihopQA validation slice, V-101's pooling, two-hop unbind-and-cleanup, n=200 per cell, three
capacity seeds. **Not analogical mapping**: V-146 is Kanerva-style holistic transformation and V-148/V-150 are
the Gayler & Levy replicator; those are different mechanisms and their exponents must never be pooled with
this one. The open problem is Kleyko et al., Survey Part I sec 4.1.

## V-152 — the comparator selected honestly. T0 / T1 / T2 / T3 ALL HOLD: the disclosed test-set handicap cost nothing

Prereg + frozen scorer + runner 4a7dbdf, committed **before** the sweep. Runner `v152_v50.py` is `v50.py`
plus a default-off `--eval_val`; the diff removes three lines, each replaced by a superset. Artifact
`v152_logs/v152.json`. 12 configurations x 3 seeds, 4.0 h wall-clock.

**Why it was run.** V-131 Part B selected the LoRA comparator on the test set and disclosed it, giving as
its reason that "this harness has no validation split, inventing one would change the training set and
break comparability". **The premise was false**: `v5.load_babi` returns `{train, val, test}`, `v50.build_rows`
calls it with `n_val=200` and returns only two of the three. The validation split was loaded and discarded
on every run. Using it costs nothing — train stays at 775 and test at 420, and passage overlap between all
three pairs is 0, measured.

    config             val (80)   test (420)   V-131b banked
    r16_e6_lr1e-4       0.9750      0.9722        0.9722
    r8_e6_lr3e-4        0.9583      0.9635        0.9635
    r32_e6_lr1e-4       0.9583      0.9540        0.9540
    r8_e6_lr1e-4        0.9333      0.9484        0.9540
    r8_e2_lr3e-4        0.9417      0.9048        0.6548   <- the one cell that did not reproduce
    r32_e2_lr1e-4       0.8958      0.9000        0.9000
    r16_e2_lr1e-4       0.7833      0.8437        0.8437
    r8_e2_lr1e-4        0.7542      0.8008        0.7952
    r16_e2_lr3e-4       0.3500      0.4056        0.4056
    r16_e6_lr3e-4       0.1375      0.1690        0.1690
    r32_e2_lr3e-4       0.1250      0.1659        0.1659
    r32_e6_lr3e-4       0.1000      0.1611        0.1611

**T0 HOLDS.** 11 of 12 reproduce within 0.02 and ten of those reproduce to four decimals exactly; the banked
best is 0.9722 against 0.9722. The single cell that does not is `r8_e2_lr3e-4` at 0.9048 against a banked
0.6548 — V-131b's run of it had a collapsed seed (0.1619) and this one did not. **That cell is a knife edge,
not a number**, and it was flagged in flight before the sweep finished rather than after.

**T1 HOLDS.** The configuration chosen as the argmax of the validation mean has a test mean of **0.9722**,
against a bar of 0.9422.

**T2 HOLDS, and it is the headline.** The validation set picks **`r16_e6_lr1e-4`** — the same configuration
the test set picks. **A legitimate procedure finds exactly what the illegitimate one found.**

**T3 HOLDS trivially, because the two selections coincide.** Margin against the honestly selected comparator
**+0.0278**; against the test-selected comparator **+0.0278**. Identical. Neither clears the manuscript's
registered ten-point bar, which is the manuscript's own finding and is unchanged. Per-seed test accuracies
of the selected configuration: 0.9714 / 0.9738 / 0.9714.

**T4, and it corrects a worry of mine.** The prereg argued that 80 rows put the standard error near 0.97 at
about 0.019, so the top configurations would not be separable and the validation argmax could easily land
elsewhere. The standard error is 0.0175 as predicted and three configurations do sit within one of it — but
the **rank correlation between validation and test across all twelve is 0.993**. The argument was right about
the top of the table and wrong about the table: the configurations span 0.10 to 0.97, so ranking them is easy
and only the very top is close, and even there the argmax landed correctly.

**Prediction accuracy.** The prereg named T2 as the one I was least sure of and argued at length that it
would probably fail. It held. I was wrong, in the direction that costs nothing.

**What the manuscript may now say.** The disclosure stays — the configuration *was* selected on the test set,
and that sentence is load-bearing and stays. What can be added is that it **made no difference**: selecting
on a held-out validation split picks the same configuration and yields the same 0.9722, so the 2.9 / 2.6 /
2.9-point margins are what an honest procedure gives, not an artifact of a generous one. This converts a
disclosed weakness into a verified non-issue, and it is the second time in two runs that a suspected
instrument fault turned out to matter in only one direction (V-151 was the other, and there it mattered a
great deal).

**What it may not say.** That the fine-tune is reliable. One of twelve configurations is a coin flip between
0.16 and 0.95 on the same seeds, four of twelve sit at 0.10-0.41, and the comparator's 0.9722 is the best of
twelve, not what a practitioner gets by default.

## 2026-10-09 — AUDIT: arena C is NOT a held-out-combination split. The manuscript's central "why VSA" claim rests its headline number on an arena where every test binding was seen in training.

Found while re-verifying, against raw artifacts and generator code rather than ledger summaries, the
conclusions I had been listing as the paper's hardest. Not an experiment: a counting audit of the data the
existing experiments ran on. No bar, no prereg; the facts below are counts and code, reproducible by the
snippets recorded in the session.

**The manuscript says** (Results, "Where the symbolic route wins decisively: combinations held out of
training"): *"Arenas B and C contain the split by construction: training contains no held-out role--filler
pair, and evaluation contains only held-out pairs."* The headline it then reports, parser 0.934 against a
10.5M LoRA at 0.515 / 0.518 / 0.515, "41.9 points behind in every seed", is **arena C**. The Discussion
builds on it: "The symbolic route's durable advantage is therefore not two-hop accuracy itself, but
generalisation to held-out symbol combinations, where the fine-tune never leaves the floor."

**Arena C has no held-out mechanism.** `v15.get_rows` builds arena B from `A11(tok, n, "train"|"eval", cfg,
seed)` with `SystematicConfig(holdout_mod=4)`, but builds arena C as `V.Arena(tok, n_tr, 42)` and
`V.Arena(tok, n_te, 4242)` -- two seeds of one generator, no split argument. `v13.Arena` draws every symbol
with `rng.randrange(N_SYM)` and every pair as `(a, rng.randrange(N_SYM))`; nothing excludes any pair from
training.

**Counted, not inferred.** N_SYM = 64, so 4,096 possible (role, filler) pairs.
- Arena C: training covers **all 4,096**; of 4,094 distinct test pairs, **100.0%** occur in training. Of the
  237 label-1 test queries, the hop-1 binding is in training 237/237, the hop-2 binding 237/237 --
  **every binding any test question traverses was seen in training.**
- Arena B: context pairs overlap heavily (94.6% of test pairs occur in training), but the **queried**
  (role, answer) pair -- the one the question is about -- is in training **0 of 241 times, 0.0%**.
  Arena B is a genuine held-out split on the binding that matters.

**So the narrative inverts.**
- On the arena that **does** hold out combinations (B), LoRA **can** solve it: .980 / .895 / .510, best
  seed within 1.6 points of the parser. The manuscript already says, correctly, that there LoRA is
  "unreliable rather than incapable".
- On the arena where LoRA **never leaves the floor** (C), there are **no** held-out combinations. LoRA's
  collapse there is therefore not a failure to generalise to unseen combinations. It is a failure to learn
  the task at all -- consistent with the record that on this family LoRA's training loss stays at 0.72-0.78
  against a chance level of 0.693, i.e. it never fits the training set either, and with V-15b, which ruled
  out budget at 5x and explicitly left "arena-C's specific format" open.

**What arena C actually measures**, and it is still a real result. Every instance carries its own 32
arbitrary role-filler bindings per level, freshly drawn, which must be read from that instance's context and
chained across two hops. The algebra does this natively; a low-rank update to a frozen model does not learn
to, even though every individual pair appears in training. That is **in-context binding of arbitrary,
instance-specific pairings** -- exactly the condition V-139 (2026-09-17) arrived at independently on natural
text, where holding out combinations did nothing to the fine-tune (gap 0.0000) because a combination-
independent rule shortcut the task. Arena C has no such rule; that, and not held-out-ness, is what separates
the arms.

**The 0.934 is genuinely the LLM-in-the-loop arm, not only the parser.** Checked separately: V-15's
probe_argmax 0.5287 was measured on a broken apparatus (`bind(v, v)` discarded every key; fix daa512c); the
re-run V-13R carried a registered regression check that parser and consistent reproduce exactly (.9340,
.9293 -- they did), and on the fixed apparatus probe_argmax = .932 / .932 / .938 = **0.9340**, tying the
parser. So the handover from frozen hidden states beats LoRA by ~42 points on arena C. The manuscript's
paragraph names the parser ("the exact-row arm ... two trainable parameters") where it should name the
handover; as written a reader takes the win to be a hand-written scanner that bypasses the language model,
which is the V-1 trap.

**Manuscript exposure** (current state v37, nothing edited by this entry):
- Results, held-out paragraph: "Arenas B and C contain the split by construction" -- FALSE for C.
- Discussion and Limitations: "durable advantage ... generalisation to held-out symbol combinations, where the
  fine-tune never leaves the floor" -- the fine-tune never leaves the floor only on the arena with no held-out
  combinations.
- Introduction contribution: "large and stable for symbol combinations held out of training" -- same.
- Abstract (v36, the submitting author's rewrite): "most pronounced when entity pairings are arbitrary,
  instance-specific, and unseen during training" -- "arbitrary, instance-specific" is right and is the real
  condition; **"unseen during training" is false for the arena that produced 0.934 vs 0.515.**
- Appendix app:heldout repeats the B-and-C claim.

**The defensible replacement claim:** on arena C, where each instance carries its own arbitrary bindings
that must be read from context and chained, the handover from frozen states reaches 0.934 and a 10.5M LoRA
stays at chance (0.515) although every binding it is tested on appears in its training data; on arena B,
the one arena that does hold out the queried binding, LoRA is unreliable rather than incapable. The
advantage is in-context binding, not generalisation to unseen combinations.

**Also recorded, a checker gap that let this through.** `verify_provenance.py` reported tab:threearena "OK,
3 file(s) verified on disk" -- it checks that declared SOURCE files exist, not that the numbers in the table
derive from them. Arena B and C's twelve values do derive from their files exactly (re-computed this
session); arena A's 0.501 does not derive from v9.json (its armB gives 0.506 final / 0.496 at epoch 1), and
four of arena A's six rows are not in that file at all. No checker reads a split's construction.

## V-153 — replication on fresh data and fresh seeds. Registered verdict: Q FAILS (my scorer could not read two of four artifacts) | C1 C2 C3 HOLD | C4 C5 VOID | N1 HOLDS | N2: LoRA does not learn arena C at all

Prereg + frozen scorer ce40da0, committed before any run; launcher run_v153.sh. Seeds 1001/2002/3003;
arena C on independent draws of data per seed (`--fresh_data`, train 100000+seed, test 200000+seed) -- the
first arena-C numbers in this project that are not one fixed draw. Scorer output: v153_logs/v153_score.out.

**The registered verdict on Q, C4 and C5 is an instrument failure, mine.** `v153_score.load` reads lists of
per-seed records; v37b.py and v58.py write `{"arms": {arm: [acc per seed]}}`. It therefore found no records in
r3_task2.json and r4_task4.json, scored R3 and R4 as VOID, and failed Q on three load-bearing arms it never
read. I had read the banked v37b.json and v58.json in exactly that dict format earlier the same session. The
verdict stands as printed; it is not edited and the scorer is not re-run under a fix.

**Values read directly from the two artifacts -- a disclosed post-hoc reading, NOT a bar verdict:**
task 2 probe_argmax 1.0/1.0/1.0 (banked 1.000), parser 1.0 x3, floor .186/.145/.179 (banked .203); task 4
probe_argmax .724/.672/.692 = .696 (banked .691), lora_direct 1.0 x3 (banked 1.000), floor .628/.634/.622
(banked .615). All within .04. Neither replication tests a manuscript claim: the code audit
(AUDIT_2026-10.md, S2) shows task 2's evaluation set is defined as the rows the regex + oracle answer
correctly, and S5 shows task 4's gap is a commutativity artifact of unmarked binding.

**What V-153 does establish, from bars the scorer read correctly, all on fresh data:**
- **C1 HOLDS** -- the projection trained through the chain loss stays at the floor (.510/.516/.512 vs floor
  .494/.514/.466).
- **C2 HOLDS** -- the handover equals the parser seed for seed (.920/.918/.904 both).
- **C3 HOLDS** -- handover minus LoRA .420/.413/.419, so the arena-C gap replicates on independent data.
  Arena-C replication of every arm within .04 of banked (parser .914 vs .934 -- slightly lower on fresh data).
- **N1 HOLDS, exactly** -- reading the query role and candidate through the identity head from their own spans
  (`probe_full`) changes nothing to the digit. The identity head's top-1 on test spans is 1.000 at context,
  query and candidate positions in all seeds (one context value .99998). So the gold-query asymmetry (audit
  "MATERIAL") is real in the code and harmless in the numbers, and "the head is perfect", previously an
  inference from probe_argmax == parser, is now measured -- including at query and candidate positions it was
  never trained on.
- **N2: LoRA does not learn the task.** Final-epoch TRAINING accuracy .532/.520/.502. The arena-C result is
  therefore not a failure to generalise -- to unseen combinations (there are none, audit 95ef459) or otherwise
  -- but a failure of a rank-16 LoRA on raw text to fit arena C's training set at the registered budget.
- **N3** -- best-minus-final-epoch gap is 0 for every arm on both sides (one seed .004). The best-epoch-on-test
  selection the audit found changed no reported number here.

**Reading.** On arena C the handover's 0.92 against LoRA's 0.50 replicates on fresh data, the identity head
reads every symbol perfectly, and LoRA cannot even fit training. That is consistent with the audit's account:
the symbolic side is handed the binding structure (spans, which tokens pair), the identity head re-identifies
tokens that are literally in the input, and the comparison is between "given the structure, compose exactly"
and "learn structure and composition from raw text with a low-rank update". It does not show that the
algebra improves the language model's own reasoning.

## B PILOT (2026-10-15) — LABELLED A PILOT, not a result. When the frozen LM parses 2WikiMultihopQA itself, every symbolic arm (VSA or table) is far below the LM's own single pass and chain of thought

Design: B_DESIGN.md. Runner b_pilot.py (smoke-tested on 2 rows first; the smoke caught a parse bug of mine --
the decomposition kept its "Start:" prefix -- fixed before the pilot). Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, greedy, 2Wiki
compositional dev rows 0-49, RAW context paragraphs with distractors. No regex, no gold spans/identities/order,
no oracle selection; gold evidences used only afterwards to score extraction. Every arm on the same 50 rows.
Value role-marked by a permutation in every HRR arm. Artifact b_logs/b_pilot.json.

    arm                       EM      F1
    direct                   .240    .394
    cot                      .320    .436
    extract + dict_exact     .060    .073
    extract + vsa_hash       .060    .073
    extract + dict_ident     .04-.08 (tau .6-.9)
    extract + vsa_ident      .04-.06
    trivial                  .000    .010
    extraction recall of gold triples .52 | start entity exact .64 | relation path exact 29/50 | 70 triples/row

Diagnostic split (uses gold only to condition, never fed to an arm): on the 11 rows where BOTH gold facts were
extracted, cot .818 vs best symbolic .364 (dict_ident) and vsa .273; on the 7 rows with facts, relations and
start all exact, cot .857 vs .286-.429. So the loss is not only extraction recall: with the right facts in hand,
lookup composition still loses -- relation names in extracted triples do not match the question's, and answer
strings differ in form.

Reading (pilot, n=50, one model, one prompt design): no sign that a VSA memory improves a frozen LM's
compositional reasoning on natural two-hop text when the LM must parse; the external route is 4-5x worse. VSA
equals the table (.06 vs .06), so superposition costs nothing here, but neither helps. 2Wiki is extraction-hard
and composition-easy (two hops, few facts); the regime where an external exact composer should help is the
reverse -- many bindings, many hops, each fact easy to extract. That is the next B experiment (arena-C-style
task, the LM extracting bindings by prompting, swept over binding count and depth), alongside a registered
version of this 2Wiki comparison on disjoint rows.

**Reading.** When a frozen 7B LM must extract and decompose natural two-hop text itself, handing composition to a
VSA memory (or to a table, which the VSA equals) makes it four to five times worse than the LM's own single pass or
CoT. The title's claim is not supported on natural two-hop text in this regime.

    relation name not matched at hop 1 / hop 2 ............ 85 / 94   (179, 60%)
    start or bridge entity under a different name, an
      alias-like subject is present ........................ 61 + 17  (78, 26%)
    start or bridge entity with no stored triples ........... 3 + 4   (7)
    walk completes .......................................... 36  (20 correct, 16 wrong)

Examples: hop-1 object "Queen Nefertari", while the next paragraph's subject is "Nefertari"; "King Bayinnaung of
Burma" against "Bayinnaung"; decomposition "place of birth or nationality" against extracted "country of citizenship";
start "Kathputli (1971 Film)" against the stored "Kathputli". The LM-embedding identity (tau .70) does not bridge
these: dict_ident 17 is below dict_exact 20.

**Reading.** On natural two-hop text, when the frozen 7B LM itself extracts and decomposes, the external-composer route
fails at **symbol grounding**: the names the LM extracts and the names it decomposes the question into do not agree
(60% relation names, 26% entity aliases). Composition is not where it fails; when the walk completes it is right 20
times out of 36. The VSA is exactly as good as a table on the same bindings (0 disagreeing rows), so superposition is
not the issue either. That holds at this load and base rate, review C1-2. Either way, the route is 3-5x worse than
the LM's own answers. The title claim has no support on this task.

This closes B1 on 2Wiki for Qwen2.5-7B. Still owed before it counts as a conclusion:
- a second model (registered separately);
- the literature check: open-IE canonicalisation and entity resolution are a known problem, and this is an instance
  of it, not a discovery.

### Literature check for the V-155/V-158 conclusion (2026-10-15) — outcome: SUPPORTED, and it is a known problem, not a finding

- **Supporting.** Open-IE triples are uncanonicalised, so the same entity or relation appears under several surface
  forms, and canonicalisation is a recognised prerequisite: Galárraga et al. 2014 (CIKM) and CESI, Vashishth, Jain &
  Talukdar, WWW 2018, pp. 1317-1327 (arXiv 1902.00172). HippoRAG (Gutiérrez et al., NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2405.14831)
  adds embedding-similarity "synonymy edges" between near-identical noun phrases for the same reason, and composes
  softly (Personalized PageRank) rather than by an exact walk. Our dict_ident/vsa_ident clustering is the analogue of
  those edges, and at tau .70 it does not bridge relation aliases.
- **No direct conflict found.** Results where KG-structured reasoning beats CoT (e.g. SG-RAG on MetaQA) use curated
  fixed-schema KGs, not LM-extracted open triples.
- **Consequence for the paper.** "The external route fails at grounding" may be stated only as an instance of the
  known canonicalisation problem, with these citations. It is not a contribution.

- Hsieh et al. 2024, RULER, variable tracking.

increment is narrower:
- the LM does all the parsing itself;
- a sharded VSA is instance-for-instance equal to a table;
- the crossover is measured on a load × depth grid under a registered bar.

### V-161 CORRECTION (2026-10-16) — the frontier "one pass" scores for Claude and DeepSeek are a parsing artifact; "frontier models fail in one pass" is WITHDRAWN as worded

Found by an independent claim-by-claim check of the compact paper (scratchpad/review_paper_compact.md, 144 claims:
97 verified, 17 wrong, 27 overstated, 3 unsupported; all addressed in paper2_compact). Re-derived by me from the raw
replies (v161_or_*.jsonl).

**What is wrong.** The registered one-pass ("direct") score reads the FIRST symbol of the reply. Claude and DeepSeek
often wrote the chain out despite "answer with only the final symbol", so their first symbol is the start and they
are scored wrong.

    reading of the direct arm      N16_H4      N64_H4      N256_H4     N16_H8      N64_H8      N256_H8
    Claude, first symbol (reg.)     47          122         150         143         150         150
    Claude, last symbol            150          150         150         150         150         150   (all bare answers correct)
    DeepSeek, first symbol (reg.)   25            2           0           1           0           0
    DeepSeek, last symbol           33          110         138          61         131         128
    DeepSeek, bare answers         25/141       2/40        0/10        1/89        0/16        0/15
    Gemini 4 (bare, 0 reasoning)   150          150         150         150         150          73
    GPT-6.1 (bare, 18-35 hidden)   150          150         150         150         150         150

**What stands.**
- Frontier models compose every chain when they write out steps, visible or hidden.
- Where one-pass behaviour is clean:
  - DeepSeek's bare answers fail beyond one hop;
  - Gemini 4, with zero reasoning tokens, composes every chain up to 1,024 facts and 73/150 at 2,048.

So "frontier models match the memory ONLY by writing out steps" is false: Gemini composes in one pass up to
1,024 facts. The supportable claim is that one-pass composition gives out at the largest load.

The registered verdicts (C3 HOLDS for DeepSeek and Gemini direct) are left as printed. DeepSeek's rests on the
artifact and is not used.

**Second-scorer limitation.** v161_indep.py used the same first-symbol rule for the direct arm, so it could not catch
this. The last-symbol and bare-answer reading above is a disclosed post-hoc second angle.
